A unified treatment of commuting tensor products of categories, operads, symmetric multicategories and their bimodules
Nicola Gambino, Richard Garner, Christina Vasilakopoulou

Abstract
. We provide a unified treatment of several commuting tensor products considered in the literature, including the tensor product of enriched categories and the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of operads and symmetric multicategories, subsuming work of Elmendorf and Mandell. We then show how a commuting tensor product extends to bimodules, generalising results of Dwyer and Hess. In particular, we construct a double category of symmetric multicategories, symmetric multifunctors and bimodules and show that it admits a symmetric oplax monoidal structure. These applications are obtained as instances of a general construction of commuting tensor products on double categories of monads, monad morphisms and bimodules.



1.
Introduction

Context, aims and motivation

Eighty years since its birth
[
EM45
]
, Category Theory continues to demonstrate the importance of abstraction and compositionality in Mathematics,
helping us to make analogies precise and to construct complex structures from simple ones. Here, we offer additional evidence of this idea, by providing a general analysis of commuting tensor products, unifying and extending a variety of results in the literature, including some by Elmendorf and Mandell
[
EM09
]
and by Dwyer and Hess
[
DH14
]
. Before describing our contributions in more detail, we provide some context and motivation.

The general idea of a commuting tensor product can be understood in a simple example. For categories
A,B,C
, a functor in two variables
(often called a sesquifunctor)
F\colon A,B\to C
consists of two families of functors,

(F(a,-)\colon B\to C)_{a\in A}
and
(F(-,b)\colon A\to C)_{b\in B}
, which agree on objects, i.e. such
that
F(a,-)(b)=F(a,-)(b)
, so that we can write
F(a,b)
for their common value for
a\in A
and
b\in B
.
We say that such
F
is commuting (or that it is a bifunctor) if for all morphisms
f\colon a\to a^{\prime}
in
A
and
g\colon b\to b^{\prime}
in
B
, the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(a,b)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(a^{\prime},b)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(a,b^{\prime})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(a^{\prime},b^{\prime})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(f,b)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(a,g)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(a^{\prime},g)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(f,b^{\prime})}

commutes. This is a commutation condition since the two paths around
the diagram involve the actions of
f
and
g
in different order
This is even more apparent when
A
,
B
and
C
are one-object
categories, hence monoids: for then,
F
is given by a pair of monoid
morphisms
f\colon A\rightarrow C
,
g\colon B\rightarrow C
, and is commuting just when
each
f(a)
commutes with each
g(b)
in
C
.
It is a classical result that, just as bilinear maps of rings are classified by
the tensor products of rings, commuting functors in two variables as above are classified by the cartesian product
A\times B
of
A
and
B
, in the sense that there is a commuting functor in two variables

A,B\to A\times B
such that composition with it induces a bijection between functors

A\times B\to C
and commuting functors in two variables
A,B\to C
, for every category
C
.

An important property of the commuting tensor product of categories is that it extends naturally to act on profunctors, also known as bimodules or distributors
[
Bén73
]
. Recall that a

[

]
.
This is in analogy with the way in which the tensor product of rings can be extended to ring bimodules.
Crucially, this involves proving a suitable interaction between composition
of profunctors and the commuting tensor product.

The initial motivation for this work was to investigate whether a similar phenomenon occurs for symmetric multicategories—also known as coloured operads
[
Yau16
]
(an operad is exactly
a symmetric multicategory with one object
[
May72
]
). Symmetric multicategories were introduced by Boardman and Vogt as part of their work on homotopy theory
[
BV73
]
, building on the notion of a
multicategory, originally defined by Lambek within categorical
logic
[
Lam69
]
. They continue to play an important role in algebraic topology to date (see
[
BM07
,
EM06
]
for example).
Much as with the situation for categories, there is a commuting tensor product for symmetric multicategories, commonly known as the Boardman–Vogt tensor product
[
BV73
]
. This can be understood
as a commuting tensor product since, for symmetric multicategories
M
and
N
, an algebra for
their tensor product
M\otimes N
is an object equipped with operations which make it into an
M
-algebra and an
N
-algebra and
commute with each other in a suitable sense. Equivalently, they are
M
-algebras in the category of
N
-algebras (and conversely). Importantly, fundamental classes of spaces can be characterised
as algebras for symmetric multicategories obtained via (derived version of) the Boardman–Vogt tensor
product (see
[
Moe23
]
for a recent overview).

There is also an analogue of profunctor between symmetric multicategories;
these were called bimodules in
[
GJ17
, Section 4.4]
, as they generalise
the operad bimodules of
[
Fre09
,
KM01
,
Rez96
]
. It is thus natural to ask
whether, just as the commuting tensor product of categories extends to profunctors, the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of symmetric multicategories extends to their bimodules. This means that, for bimodules

\lxSVG@closescope {{

, interacting suitably with composition of bimodules.
The only result in this direction that we are aware of was obtained by Dwyer and Hess in
[
DH14
]
, where they showed that the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of
(single-coloured)
operads
extends to their bimodules. Even in the case of operads, however, it is not known what kind of monoidal structure this is and how it interacts with the composition of bimodules. This paper provides
answers to these questions.

Our first goal in this paper is to provide a unified account of a variety of commuting tensor products of the kind
described above for categories and symmetric multicategories. Our results will unify several
known results and derive some new ones.
Our second goal is to show that, in the general setting of our analysis, commuting tensor products can be extended to act on bimodules. As an application, we will show that the Boardman–Vogt tensor product extends to bimodules (which we will call
symmetric multiprofunctors
here, to highlight the analogy with profunctors), extending the work of Dwyer and Hess. We will also establish the kind of monoidal
structure this gives rise to, in particular describing precisely the interaction of the Boardman–Vogt tensor product with the composition of symmetric multiprofunctors.

This work therefore contributes to the study of the bicategory of
of symmetric sequences
[
FGHW08
]
and the bicategory of
symmetric multicategories and symmetric multiprofunctors
[
GJ17
]
,
which have attracted significant interest in recent years, thanks to the
applications they have found in algebraic topology, mathematical logic and theoretical
computer science. Indeed, these bicategories have been shown to admit a rich structure, including being cartesian closed
[
FGHW08
,
GJ17
]
,
to admit fixpoint operators
[
Gal23
]
, and support a notion of differentiation
[
FGH24
]
.
Our work here extends this work by showing the existence of additional structure on the double
in which these bicategories naturally embed, which we hope will foster new applications.

Commuting and non-commuting tensor products.

Main results

In order to develop our general analysis of commuting tensor products,
we shall work in the setting of a double category
[
Ehr63
]
, in which one has two classes of morphisms, vertical and horizontal. This is useful for us because it matches our examples, where one has two kinds of maps, e.g. functors and profunctors. Another feature of double categories that is important for us is that they provide a a more general and convenient framework for
the construction of monoidal structures than bicategories
[
GG09
,
HS19
]
, cf. our comments below.

Crucially for our purposes, the double categories
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{Mod}
,
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}
and
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{MultProf}
(whose definitions are outlined in
Table

1
) can be described
homogeneously. For a double category
\mathbb{C}
with stable local reflexive coequalisers, there is a double category
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
with horizontal monads in
\mathbb{C}
as objects,
monad morphisms as vertical maps, and monad bimodules as horizontal maps
[
CS10
,
Shu08
]
.
If
\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
, the double category of matrices, then
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})=\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}
. In particular, as is
well-known, monads in
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
are categories. If
\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}
, the double category of symmetric sequences
[
GGV24
]
, then
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})=\mathbb{S}\mathsf{MultProf}
. In particular, monads in
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}
are symmetric multicategories. In light of this, our unified treatment will be achieved by understanding under what assumptions on a double category
\mathbb{C}
one can define a ‘commuting’ tensor product on the double category
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
. Our theory will apply also to the
\mathcal{V}
-enriched versions of the examples above, where
\mathcal{V}
is a fixed symmetric monoidal category satisfying appropriate axioms. We will
write
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
for the enriched counterpart of
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
and use similar notation for the other double
categories under consideration.

To achieve our goal, we shall extend the analysis of commutativity carried out in
[
GL16
]
.
This work was developed
in the context of a normal duoidal category, i.e. a category equipped with two monoidal structures
(\mathcal{E},\circ,J,\boxtimes,I)
related by (not necessarily invertible) interchange
maps, subject to appropriate axioms; for example, any symmetric (or braided) monoidal category is normal duoidal, with the two tensor products taken to be the same. One of the main theorems in
[
GL16
]
shows that, for a normal duoidal category
\mathcal{E}
satisfying appropriate assumptions, the category of
\circ
-monoids and
\circ
-monoid morphisms in
\mathcal{E}
admits a ‘commuting’ monoidal structure
\otimes
such that
\circ
-monoid maps
A\otimes B\rightarrow C
classify pairs of
\circ
-monoid maps
A\rightarrow C
,
B\rightarrow C
which commute with respect to the other tensor product
\boxtimes
of
\mathcal{E}
. Here, the meaning of “commuting” generalises the motivating case of monoids in
(\mathsf{Set},\times,1,\times,1)
, for which it means “with images that commute elementwise”.

This result of
[
GL16
]
, applied to suitable bases
\mathcal{E}
, provides a unified treatment of the commuting tensor product of operads and Lawvere theories, but does not apply to categories or symmetric multicategories. Now,
[
GL16
]
also considers a more general situation which, rather than the category of
\circ
-monoids, starts from the category of
(\mathcal{E},\circ,J)
-enriched categories, and constructs a ‘commuting’ tensor product thereon. Applied to
(\mathsf{Set},\times,1,\times,1)
, this reconstructs perfectly the commuting tensor product (= cartesian product) of categories, and more generally, the usual tensor product of
\mathcal{V}
-categories over a symmetric (or braided) monoidal base
\mathcal{V}
. Yet even this generalisation does not suffice to capture symmetric multicategories, which are not
\mathcal{V}
-categories for any known enrichment base
\mathcal{V}
.

Thus, our development will provide a different generalisation of the ‘one-object’ results of
[
GL16
]
to the ‘many-object’ case.
We will replace the monoidal category
(\mathcal{E},\circ,J)
with a double category
\mathbb{C}
, using the horizontal composition in
\mathbb{C}
as the counterpart of the substitution monoidal structure of
\mathcal{E}
and correspondingly, replacing
\circ
-monoids in
the monoidal category with horizontal monads in the double category (see
Section

2
for details).
The second monoidal structure
\boxtimes
on the duoidal category
\mathcal{E}
is then replaced by a
normal oplax monoidal structure

[
GGV24
]

on the double category
\mathbb{C}
.
Here, the oplaxity means that the functoriality of the tensor functor holds only up to an interchange 2-cell of the form

(1)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}\boxtimes C_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}\boxtimes C_{2}\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(y_{1}\circ x_{1})\boxtimes(y_{2}\circ x_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\xi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{1}\boxtimes x_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{1}\boxtimes y_{2}}

For example, any symmetric monoidal double category
\mathbb{C}
is normal oplax monoidal. In particular, if

\mathcal{V}
is a symmetric monoidal category, then the double category
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
is symmetric monoidal in an evident way, and hence normal oplax monoidal. Less trivially,
[
GGV24
]
showed that, for a
cartesian
monoidal category
\mathcal{V}
, the double category of
\mathcal{V}
-enriched symmetric sequences
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
is normal oplax monoidal under a tensor product
\boxtimes
which generalises the
arithmetic product
of one-object symmetric sequences from
[
DH14
]
.

In the context of a normal oplax monoidal double category, we introduce a notion of a monad multimorphism, by extending to the abstract
setting the concept of a functor in many variables, and say what it means for a monad multimorphism to be commuting, by generalising the definition for a family of monoid morphisms to be commuting in
[
GL16
]
.
The essential content of this definition can be understood in the binary case, as follows. First of all, a binary monad multimorphism
(f,\phi,\psi)\colon(A,a),(B,b)\to(C,c)
involves a vertical map
f\colon A\boxtimes B\rightarrow C
and monad maps
(f,\phi)\colon(A\boxtimes B,a\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B})\rightarrow(C,c)
and
(f,\psi)\colon(A\boxtimes B,\mathrm{id}_{A}\boxtimes b)\rightarrow(C,c)
. Now such a multimorphism is said to be commuting if

where the 2-cells
\sigma
and
\tau
can be
obtained via the interchange 2-cell
\xi
in (
1
).
Here, commutativity can be intuitively seen by the swapping of
\phi
and
\psi
between
the two diagrams (see
3.1.2
and
4.1.4
for details).
As we will see, this captures the appropriate
notions of commutativity in the examples of interest. Our motivating question then becomes one of identifying conditions under which commuting monad multimorphisms can be classified, meaning that
there exists a monad
(A,a)\otimes(B,b)
with a commuting multimorphism

(A,a),(B,b)\to(A,a)\otimes(B,b)
which is
universal
, in that it induces, via composition, a bijection between monad morphisms

(A,a)\otimes(B,b)\to(C,c)
and commuting monad multimorphisms

(A,a),(B,b)\to(C,c)
for every monad
(C,c)
.

Our first main result,
4.3.6
, shows that, under appropriate assumptions,
the category of
monads and monad morphisms in
\mathbb{C}
, i.e. the vertical category of
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
,
admits a commuting tensor product, which is moreover part of a symmetric monoidal
closed structure. When applied to the normal oplax monoidal double category of matrices
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
,
this gives back the tensor product of enriched categories and enriched
functors. When applied to the normal oplax monoidal double category of symmetric sequences
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
, this
gives back the construction of the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of enriched symmetric multicategories and symmetric multifunctors obtained in
[
EM09
]
.
The second main result proved here,
5.4.2
, shows that
the commuting tensor product of
4.3.6
extends to monad
bimodules and that the double category
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
of bimodules in
\mathbb{C}

admits a symmetric oplax monoidal structure.

We then provide two applications of our main results. First, we consider the double category of matrices
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
. When
\mathcal{V}
is symmetric monoidal, our results then give an abstract construction of the tensor product of
\mathcal{V}
-categories and its
extension to profunctors (
6.1.3
). While this is known, it is pleasing to have a conceptual
proof of the existence of the symmetric monoidal structure on the bicategory of
\mathcal{V}
-profunctors, in
particular taking care of the daunting coherence axioms.
However, when
\mathcal{V}
is merely normal duoidal, we still have normal oplax monoidal structure on
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
, and in this context, we re-find exactly the previous ‘many-object’ theory of commutativity developed in
[
GL16
]
—but, in addition, an extension of that theory to bimodules between enriched categories, which appears to be new.

For our second main application, we consider the normal oplax monoidal double category of symmetric sequences
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
. As noted above, our results here give
back the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multicategories, but furthermore provide a new result
in extending it to their bimodules, which we we call here
symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multiprofunctors
(
6.2.8
).
Our approach with double categories is useful here: the double category
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{MultProf}_{\mathcal{V}}
admits a symmetric oplax monoidal structure that does not seem to satisfy the
extra condition of normality that is needed in order to obtain a symmetric monoidal structure on its horizontal bicategory (cf.
5.4.3
).

Even when restricted to operads (
6.2.10
), this provides something new, in that it describes precisely
the interaction between the Boardman–Vogt tensor product and the composition operation of bimodules.
Given that the definition of the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of operads and operad morphisms goes back to
[
BV73
]
and its extension to operad bimodules to
[
DH14
]
, this
appears to fill a gap in our knowledge of operads.

Let us also remark that our theory can be applied to yield commuting
tensor products for variants of symmetric multicategories, such as cartesian multicategories
[
Lam89
]
and potentially also to their affine and relevant counterparts, which are of interest in mathematical logic
and theoretical computer science
[
Oli21
]
. Indeed, cartesian multicategories with a single object
are exactly Lawvere theories
[
Law63
]
. Since this requires substantial additional work, we do not include it here.

Technical aspects

Our main results establish the definition and key properties of the commuting tensor product of monads
and of bimodules. However, they come at the end of a development that involves
a number of auxiliary notions and results, some of which may be of independent interest.
Throughout, we have found it useful to use symmetric multicategories not only as source of examples, but also as tool in our proofs. Thus, rather than construct symmetric monoidal structures on a category directly,
we instead enhance the category to a
symmetric multicategory and apply the notion of representability due to Hermida
[
Her00
]
. This not only matches naturally what
happens in examples, but allows us to organise some of the more complex
proofs in conceptual terms.

As a first step, we construct and study the symmetric multicategory of monads and
(not necessarily commuting) monad multimorphisms. In particular, we show that, under suitable hypotheses on our base double category
\mathbb{C}
,
this symmetric multicategory is closed and representable. We obtain
what may be called the non-commuting tensor product of monads (
3.3.11
).
In the example of
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
, where monads are enriched categories, this gives back what is sometimes called the “funny tensor product”
of enriched categories
[
Str96
]
, whose internal hom consists of functors and not-necessarily-natural
transformations. In the example of
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
, where monads are symmetric multicategories,
this is the auxiliary tensor product written
M\sharp N
in
[
EM09
]
, cf.
Table

1
.

Building on this, we introduce our notion of a commuting monad multimorphism (
4.1.4
) and proceed in parallel to what we did for the non-commuting tensor
product. In particular, we introduce a symmetric multicategory of monads and
commuting monad multimorphisms and prove that it is closed and representable.
While we can leverage the earlier work on non-commuting tensor product to simplify
some of the work, the results here involve several additional delicate checks on the preservation of
commutativity by the transposition operations that are involved in the representability.

We next turn to extending the commuting tensor product to bimodules, abstracting and generalising the work of Dwyer and Hess in
[
DH14
]
. We use the multicategorical approach again,
introducing a notion of commuting bimodule morphism and showing that it can be classified. This may be of interest in that it gives a universal characterisation of the commuting tensor product of bimodules, an aspect which was not considered in
[
DH14
]
. We then study the interaction between the composition of bimodules and the commuting tensor of monads, showing that we have the structure of symmetric oplax monoidal double category. Here, it should be pointed out that the interaction between the composition of bimodules and the commuting tensor of monads is entirely novel and
was not considered, even in the case of operads, in
[
DH14
]
.

Last, but not least, when it comes to examples, we will have to carry out some additional work to
ensure that the hypotheses of our theorems are satisfied. For
our application to symmetric multicategories, we extend the work in
[
GGV24
]
and
show that the oplax monoidal structure double category
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
of symmetric sequences is symmetric and closed, a result that is of independent
interest as it generalises the ‘divided powers’ closed structure of
[
DH14
]
.

Outline

Section

2
sets out the preliminaries needed for the paper, including
the key facts from
[
GGV24
]
that we will use. In
Section

3
we construct the
non-commuting tensor product of monads. This is then used in
Section

4
to define
the commuting tensor product. We extend this to bimodules in
Section

5
. We end
the paper in
Section

6
with applications.

2.
Monads and bimodules in double categories

2.1.
Double categories and fibrant double categories

We begin by recalling the notion of (pseudo) double category

[
GP99
,
HS19
]
, in part to establish
our notational conventions.

Definition 2.1.1
.

A
double category

\mathbb{C}
consists of a graph of categories

\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathbb{C}_{0}
, together with composition and identity functors

\circ\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\times_{\mathbb{C}_{0}}\mathbb{C}_{1}\to\mathbb{C}_{1}
and

\mathrm{id}\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}\to\mathbb{C}_{1}
which are associative and unital up
to coherent natural isomorphism. We refer to objects

A,B,\dots
and morphisms
f,g,\dots\colon A\rightarrow B
of

\mathbb{C}_{0}
as
objects
and
vertical
1
-cells
of
\mathbb{C}
,
and refer to objects
x,y,\dots
and morphisms

\alpha,\beta,\dots\colon x\rightarrow y
of
\mathbb{C}_{1}
as

horizontal
1
-cells
and
2
-morphisms
of
\mathbb{C}
. We
typically write horizontal
1
-cells as
x\colon A\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow B
to
indicate that
\mathfrak{s}(x)=A
and
\mathfrak{t}(x)=B
, and
write
2
-morphisms
\alpha\colon x\rightarrow y
as to the left in:

(2)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}

to indicate that
\mathfrak{s}(\alpha)=f
and

\mathfrak{t}(\alpha)=g
. The invertible witnesses to the weak
associativity of composition and identities are so-called

globular

2
-morphisms, i.e., ones living in the fibres of
the functor

(\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t})\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}\times\mathbb{C}_{0}
; a typical globular
2
-morphism is displayed to the
right above. We will not name these globular coherence cells, and
will typically suppress associativity isomorphisms
completely.

In order to illustrate the notions to be introduced throughout the
paper, we begin here the development of a simple running example. As
the paper progresses, we will slowly add further hypotheses to this
example, in parallel with the hypotheses we require in the general theory.

Running Example 2.1.2
.

Let
\mathcal{V}
be a monoidal category with coproducts preserved by tensor product in each variable. We write
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
for the double category of
\mathcal{V}
-matrices with sets as objects, functions as vertical maps, and
\mathcal{V}
-matrices as horizontal maps. Explicitly, a
\mathcal{V}
-matrix
x\colon A\hbox to38pt{\vbox to5.6pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 18.99997pt\lower-0.5pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{}{}{}{}{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}}{{}}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{}{{
{}{}}}{
{}{}}

1

For example, in

, we have

(3)

and
\mathcal{H}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
is the bicategory of matrices, see
[
Bén73
,

]
.

Fibrancy is one of the most fundamental assumptions
we make on our base double category. It is useful for numerous reasons, for example since
it often allows us to deduce “global”
universal properties from “local” ones, cf.
2.2.6
below.

Definition 2.1.3
.

A double category
\mathbb{C}
is
fibrant
if

(\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t})\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}\times\mathbb{C}_{0}
is a Grothendieck fibration.

A fibrant double category is the same as a
framed bicategory
in
the sense of
[
Shu08
, Section 4]
, and as shown in
Theorem 4.1 of
op. cit.
, there are various ways of
reformulating the condition. In particular, we have for any vertical

1
-cell
f\colon A\rightarrow B
, a pair of horizontal
1
-cells

\wh{f}\colon A\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow B
and
\wc{f}\colon B\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow A

and associated

2
-morphisms
p_{1}
and
q_{1}
, obtained as cartesian liftings of

\mathrm{id}_{B}\in\mathbb{C}_{1}
along the maps
(f,1)
and
(1,f)
in
\mathbb{C}_{0}\times\mathbb{C}_{0}
, as to the left in:

2.2.
Monads

In this paper we will be concerned with monads (and later bimodules)

[

•

(A,x)

monad map

(f,\phi)
between monads
(A,a,\mu,\eta)

and
(B,b,\mu,\eta)

We write
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
for the category of monads and monad maps in

\mathbb{C}
. We will generally write objects of
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
as
(A,a)
,
suppressing the multiplication and unit
2
-morphisms.

Running Example 2.2.2
.

The double category
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}})
is the category of
\mathcal{V}
-graphs, i.e., pairs of a set
A
of “vertices” and an
A\times A
-indexed set of “
\mathcal{V}
-objects of edges” between them. On the other hand, a monad
(A,a)
in
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
is precisely a
\mathcal{V}
-category
\mathcal{A}
with object-set
A
, and hom-sets
\mathcal{A}(x,y)=a[x;y]
. The
2
-morphisms
\mu
and
\eta
provide the composition and identities, for which the monad axioms express associativity and unitality. A monad map
(f,\phi)\colon(A,a)\rightarrow(B,b)
is precisely a
\mathcal{V}
-functor
\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
, with action on objects
f
and action on homs
\phi
. Therefore
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}})=\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
.

We have a commutative triangle of forgetful functors

(6)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{0}\mathrlap{,}}

where the map across the top forgets the monad structure, and the maps
down to
\mathbb{C}_{0}
forget the horizontal structure. We will write

\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
and
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
for the fibre categories of
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
and
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})

over
A\in\mathbb{C}_{0}
. Note that
\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
is the hom-category
\mathbb{C}[A,A]
;
and, if we
view
\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
as monoidal under horizontal composition
\circ
, then
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})

is precisely the category of
\circ
-monoids in
\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
.

Remark 2.2.3
.

It is a trivial, but important, observation that the forgetful
functor
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
has a left adjoint
\Delta
.
This adjoint sends
A\in\mathbb{C}_{0}
to the identity monad

\Delta_{A}=(A,\mathrm{id}_{A})
, with unit and multiplication given by the
appropriate coherence constraints in
\mathbb{C}
. When
\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
,
this
\Delta_{A}
is equally well the discrete
\mathcal{V}
-category on the
set
A
, and so we may refer to
\Delta_{A}
as the
discrete
monad on
A
.

The preceding remark tells us that the free monad on an object of

\mathbb{C}_{0}
always exists. However, in this paper, we will also require
free monads on endomaps, whose existence is an extra hypothesis – see also
[
FGK11
, Def. 2.8]
.

Definition 2.2.4
.

We say that the double category
\mathbb{C}

admits free monads
if the forgetful functor
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})

in
Eq.

6
has a left adjoint over
\mathbb{C}_{0}
.

This definition expresses the familiar universal property of a free
monad on an endomap, and will be used in
Section

4
to
construct commuting tensor products of monads. However, it is often
easier in practice to verify the weaker condition that each forgetful
functor
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
has a left adjoint for every
A\in\mathbb{C}
. For example,
in
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
, an object of
\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
is a
\mathcal{V}
-graph

x\in[A\times A,{\mathcal{V}}]
, and the free monad thereon is given by
the
usual free
\mathcal{V}
-category
\mathcal{X}\in\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
on this
\mathcal{V}
-graph (see e.g.
[
Wol74
]
), with homs

\mathcal{X}(a,a^{\prime})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{0},\dots,a_{n}\in A\\
a_{0}=a,a_{n}=a^{\prime}\end{subarray}}x[a_{n-1};a_{n}]\otimes\cdots\otimes x[a_{0};a_{1}]

However, the weaker condition just described will imply the stronger
property of
2.2.4
if the double category
\mathbb{C}
is
fibrant.
This result is due
to
[
FGK11
]
; we sketch the proof as we will need some
of the details. Most importantly, we will have further use for the
following lemma:

Lemma 2.2.5
.

Assume
\mathbb{C}
is fibrant. The functor
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathbb{C}_{0}
is a bifibration,
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathbb{C}_{0}
is a fibration and the
triangle
Eq.

6
is a fibred functor.

Proof.

Since
(\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t})
is a Grothendieck bifibration,
so is its pullback
\pi\colon\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
as
in
Eq.

4
. Each fibre category
\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})=\mathbb{C}[A,A]

is, as noted above, monoidal under
\circ
, and for any

f\colon A\rightarrow B
in
\mathbb{C}_{0}
, the reindexing functor

\wh{f}\circ({\mathord{\text{--}}})\circ\wc{f}\colon\mathsf{End}_{B}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
can be made lax monoidal via the globular
2
-morphisms

p_{1}\circ q_{1}\colon\wh{f}\circ\wc{f}\Rightarrow\mathrm{id}_{B}
and

q_{2}\circ p_{2}\colon\mathrm{id}_{A}\Rightarrow\wc{f}\circ\wh{f}
. It
follows that taking monoids in each fibre yields a new fibration
over the same base; this fibration is easily seen to be

\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
, which is thus a Grothendieck fibration,
with
Eq.

6
being the fibred forgetful
functor. For more details, we refer the reader
to
[
FGK11
, §3]
and
[
Vas19
, §3.2]
.
∎

From this, we quickly conclude:

Proposition 2.2.6
.

Assume
\mathbb{C}
is fibrant and that for every
A\in\mathbb{C}
, the forgetful functor
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
has a left adjoint.
Then
\mathbb{C}
admits free monads, namely those local free objects have the stronger universal property of providing the values of a left adjoint to the functor

\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
.

Proof.

The result follows from the fact that a fibred functor between
fibrations has a left adjoint if and only if it has a left adjoint
on each fibre; see, for example
[
Bor94
, Proposition 8.4.2]

or
[
Jac99
, Lemma 1.8.9]
2
2

2

Note that these references
assume a further Beck–Chevalley condition on the fibrewise left
adjoints, and conclude that the global left adjoint is itself a
fibred functor; however, an inspection of the proofs show that
they carry through without these further assumptions on each side.
Indeed, the weaker result can be seen as a special case of the

doctrinal adjunction
of
[
Kel74
]
.

.
∎

2.3.
Bimodules

\mathbb{C}
, the category of
monads in
\mathbb{C}
is the category of objects and vertical
morphisms of a new double category
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
, whose horizontal arrows
are the
bimodules
between monads:

Proposition 2.3.3

(Shulman)
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a double
category with stable local reflexive coequalisers. There is a double
category
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
with monad as objects, monad morphisms as vertical

\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
itself has stable local
reflexive coequalisers.

Proof.

The proof in
[
Shu08
, Theorem 11.5]
carries
over. The development therein assumes stable local coequalisers,
rather than stable local
reflexive
coequalisers, but only
only the latter are used. Of course, since we only assume stable
local reflexive coequalisers, that is all we get in
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
as well.
∎

Moreover, we have:

Proposition 2.3.4

(Shulman)
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a double
category with stable local reflexive coequalisers. If
\mathbb{C}
is
fibrant, then so is
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
. ∎

Thus, for instance, we deduce in the situation of our running example
that

is fibrant when it exists.

Remark 2.3.6
.

The restriction to stable local reflexive coequalisers (in
2.3.3
) rather than all coequalisers is necessary for
our applications in
Section

6
. Indeed, we will see
there that the double category
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
of categorical symmetric
sequences has all local coequalisers, but only the reflexive ones
need be stable.

We now recall the construction of free bimodules and some of their properties, as these will play an important
role in our development. We write

U\colon\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathbb{C}

for the evident forgetful double functor, whose components fit into the commutative diagram of categories and (ordinary) functors

(9)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})_{0}\times\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{0}\times\mathbb{C}_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U_{0}\times U_{0}}

which amounts to
U=(U_{0},U_{1})
preserving source and target. Notice that
U_{0}\colon\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathbb{C}_{0}
coincides with the left leg of
Eq.

6
.

Let
(A,a)
and
(B,b)
be monads. By the notation introduced in
Section

2
,
the hom-category
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})[(A,a),(B,b)]
has
(b,a)
-bimodules as objects
and globular bimodule 2-morphisms as maps. There is a
forgetful functor

U_{a,b}\colon\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})[(A,a),(B,b)]\to\mathbb{C}[A,B]

mapping a bimodule to its underlying horizontal map and a bimodule 2-morphism to its underlying 2-morphism.

Lemma 2.3.7
.

The functor

is monadic.

The functor

{{}}
}
\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope }
\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}(B^{\prime},b^{\prime})
is a bimodule.
This can be shown using companions and conjoints and
2.3.7
, crucially exploiting the compatibility of forgetful functor
U
with companions and conjoints.
∎

2.4.
Limits and colimits in a double category

For many constructions in this paper, we will require various kinds of
completeness and cocompleteness of our base double category. Firstly,
we have notions which relate to “ordinary”
1
-categorical limits
and colimits.

Definition 2.4.1
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a double category, and let
\mathcal{D}
be a class of
diagram-shapes (i.e., a class of small categories).

•

We say that
\mathbb{C}
has
parallel

\mathcal{D}
-(co)limits
if
\mathbb{C}_{1}
and
\mathbb{C}_{0}
are
equipped with chosen (co)limits of
\mathcal{D}
-shaped diagrams, and
these are preserved strictly by the source and target functors

\mathfrak{s}
and
\mathfrak{t}
.

•

We say that
\mathbb{C}
has
local
\mathcal{D}
-(co)limits

if each hom-category
\mathbb{C}[A,B]
is equipped with chosen
(co)limits of
\mathcal{D}
-shaped diagrams. We say that these local
(co)limits are
stable
if they are preserved by each pre-
and postcomposition functor
\mathbb{C}[A,B]\rightarrow\mathbb{C}[A^{\prime},B]
and

\mathbb{C}[A,B]\rightarrow\mathbb{C}[A,B^{\prime}]
.

The term “parallel (co)limit” is due to Paré, see also
[
ASV24
, Def. 3.1.9]
. In fact, the strict preservation of chosen (co)limits by
\mathfrak{s}
and
\mathfrak{t}
is ensured when
\mathbb{C}
is fibrant and
\mathfrak{s}
and
\mathfrak{t}
preserve (co)limits in the usual – up to isomorphism – sense.
Moreover, notice that what we here call “stable local” (co)limits are elsewhere called only “local”, see e.g.
[
Shu08
, Def. 11.4]
, and coincide with what are commonly termed local (co)limits in the horizontal bicategory.

Parallel limits and colimits are “global”, and so it should not be a
surprise that we can use fibrancy to deduce their existence from that
of “local” limits and colimits.

Lemma 2.4.2
.

Assume that
\mathbb{C}
is fibrant and let
\mathcal{D}
be a class of
diagram-shapes. If
\mathbb{C}_{0}
has
\mathcal{D}
-(co)limits, and
\mathbb{C}
has local

\mathcal{D}
-(co)limits, then
\mathbb{C}
has parallel
\mathcal{D}
-(co)limits.

Thus, in our running example of
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
, if
\mathcal{V}
has

\mathcal{D}
-(co)limits, then each hom-category

\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}[A,B]=\mathcal{V}^{B\times A}
will have

\mathcal{D}
-(co)limits; whence by this result
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
will have
parallel
\mathcal{D}
-(co)limits.

Proof.

The following is a standard fact about Grothendieck bifibrations

p\colon\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
: if
\mathcal{B}
has a choice of

\mathcal{D}
-(co)limits, and each fibre category
\mathcal{E}_{b}
has a
choice of
\mathcal{D}
-(co)limits, then the total category
\mathcal{E}

has a choice of
\mathcal{D}
-(co)limits that is strictly preserved
by
p
3
3

3

This can be deduced, for example, from
[
Her94
, Cor. 3.7]
together with the fact that in a bifibration, reindexing functors for the fibration and the opfibration structure are adjoints to one another. See also
[
ASV24
, Prop. 3.1.13]
.
. Apply this fact to the bifibration

(\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t})\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}\times\mathbb{C}_{0}
, whose fibre categories are
\mathbb{C}[A,B]
.
∎

In this paper we will also make use of limits and colimits in
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})

and
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
. The following lemma allows us to ensure the necessary
completeness and cocompleteness, see also
[
ASV24
, Prop. 3.1.11&3.3.6]
.

Lemma 2.4.3
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a double category, and
\mathcal{D}
a class of diagram-shapes.

(1)

If
\mathbb{C}
has parallel
\mathcal{D}
-(co)limits, then
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})

has
\mathcal{D}
-(co)limits strictly preserved by
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
.

(2)

If
\mathbb{C}
has parallel
\mathcal{D}
-limits, then
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})

has
\mathcal{D}
-limits which are strictly preserved by
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
.

(3)

If
\mathbb{C}
has stable local reflexive coequalisers, free
monads, and local
\mathcal{D}
-colimits, then each
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
has
\mathcal{D}
-colimits.

For example, if
\mathcal{V}
has reflexive coequalisers preserved by tensor
in each variable, then
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
will have stable local reflexive
coequalisers, and we have already seen that it has free monads. Thus,
each
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
will have any class of colimits that
\mathcal{V}
has.

Proof.

For (i), the assumptions imply that (
4
) is a
pullback of strict
\mathcal{D}
-(co)limit-preserving functors: whence the
pullback category
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
also has
\mathcal{D}
-(co)limits which are
preserved by the projections to
\mathbb{C}_{0}
and
\mathbb{C}_{1}
.
For (ii), it is easy to see that, under no assumptions at all,
the forgetful functor
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
creates limits
strictly; now combine this with (i).

For (iii), the assumptions imply that each
\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})=\mathbb{C}[A,A]
has reflexive
coequalisers preserved by the composition monoidal structure. It
follows by
[
Por19
, Theorem 2.3]
that the category of monoids
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
has all
coequalisers. Now since
U\colon\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
has, as a result of our assumptions (
2.2.4
), a left adjoint
F
, it is monadic. It follows by
the argument of
[
Lin69
]
that
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
has all

\mathcal{D}
-colimits, since
\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
does; explicitly, for
\mathcal{I}\in\mathcal{D}
,
the colimit of a diagram
D\colon\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})

can be
computed as the coequaliser of the parallel arrows

\displaystyle F(\mathrm{colim}(UFUD))

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\hskip 16.38895pt\hskip 16.38895pt\ \ \hskip 8.19447ptF(\mathrm{colim}(U\varepsilon_{D}))\hskip 16.38895pt\hskip 16.38895pt\ \ \hskip 8.19447pt}F(\mathrm{colim}(UD))\qquad\text{and}

\displaystyle F(\mathrm{colim}(UFUD))

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{F(\text{can})}FUF(\mathrm{colim}(UD))\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_{UF(\mathrm{colim}(UD))}}F(\mathrm{colim}(UD))

in
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
, where

\text{can}\colon\mathrm{colim}(UFUD)\rightarrow UF(\mathrm{colim}\ D)
is the canonical comparison map.
∎

The following lemma that concerns connected colimits in the fibre and total category of
\mathbb{C}_{1}
and
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
above
\mathbb{C}_{0}
, will also be of use.
Notice that here, colimits in the base category are not required.

Lemma 2.4.4
.

Assume that
\mathbb{C}
is fibrant and that
\mathcal{D}
is a class of

connected
diagram-shapes. Then

(1)

a
\mathcal{D}
-colimit in
\mathbb{C}[A,B]
is a colimit in
\mathbb{C}_{1}
, and

(2)

a
\mathcal{D}
-colimit in
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
is a colimit in
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
.

In particular, if
\mathbb{C}
has local
\mathcal{D}
-colimits (resp., each

\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
has
\mathcal{D}
-colimits) then
\mathbb{C}_{1}
(resp.,
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
)
has colimits of all identity-on-objects
\mathcal{D}
-shaped diagrams.

Proof.

This follows from another general fact about Grothendieck fibrations

p\colon\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
: namely, that the colimit of a
connected diagram
D\colon\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{b}
in any
fibre category is also a colimit in
\mathcal{E}
. Applying this to the
fibrations

(\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t})\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\to\mathbb{C}_{0}\times\mathbb{C}_{0}
and

\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathbb{C}_{0}
yields the result.

To verify the general fact, let

\bigl(q_{i}\colon Di\rightarrow\mathrm{colim}(D)\bigr)
be a colimiting cocone in

\mathcal{E}_{b}
, and
(f_{i}\colon Di\rightarrow W)
any cocone under

D
in
\mathcal{E}
. By connectedness, we must have that

p(f_{i})=p(f_{j})\colon b\rightarrow p(W)
for all

i,j\in\mathcal{I}
. Thus, by the universal property of
reindexing we have the first natural bijection in:

[\mathcal{I},\mathcal{E}](D,\Delta W)\cong\sum_{h\colon b\rightarrow pW}[\mathcal{I},\mathcal{E}_{b}](D,\Delta(h^{\ast}W))\cong\sum_{h\colon b\rightarrow pW}\mathcal{E}_{b}(\mathrm{colim}(D),h^{\ast}W)\cong\mathcal{E}(\mathrm{colim}(D),W)

wherein the other bijections are the universal property of the
colimit, and the universal property of reindexing again.
It follows
that
\bigl(q_{i}\colon Di\rightarrow\mathrm{colim}(D)\bigr)
is
also a colimit in
\mathcal{E}
.
∎

Finally in this section, we record an additional kind of limit,
peculiar to double categories, which will be used in this paper; see
[
Nie12
, Prop. 4.1]
.

Definition 2.4.5
.

A double category
\mathbb{C}
has
1-tabulators
if the
identities functor
\mathrm{id}\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{1}
has a
right adjoint
T\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
. More explicitly,
this means that for every horizontal arrow
x\colon A\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow B
of
\mathbb{C}
,
there is an object
Tx\in\mathbb{C}
, called the
1
-tabulator
of
x
,
equipped with a
2
-morphism

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Tx}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Tx}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{Tx}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{\mathfrak{s}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\pi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{\mathfrak{t}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}

which is universal among
2
-morphisms into
x
from a horizontal
identity
1
-cell.

2.5.
Normal oplax monoidal structure

The other main requirement we will impose on our base double category
is what in
[
GGV24
]
was termed
normal oplax monoidal
structure
. In this section, we recall the relevant definitions, and
extend these by introducing notions of
closedness
and

symmetry
for normal oplax monoidal double categories, generalising
those for (pseudo) monoidal double categories.

In the following definition, we make use of the standard notions of

oplax double functor
and
vertical transformation
; see,
for example,
[
GGV24
, Definitions. 3.1 & 3.5]
.

Definition 2.5.1
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a double category. An
oplax monoidal structure
on
\mathbb{C}
consists of:

•

an oplax double functor
\boxtimes\colon\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}
;

•

an oplax double functor
I\colon\mathbf{1}\to\mathbb{C}
; and

•

invertible vertical transformations
\alpha\colon\mathord{\boxtimes}\circ(1\times\mathord{\boxtimes})\Rightarrow\mathord{\boxtimes}\circ(\mathord{\boxtimes}\times 1)
,

\lambda\colon\mathord{\boxtimes}\circ(I\times 1)\Rightarrow 1
and
\rho\colon\mathord{\boxtimes}\circ(1\times I)\Rightarrow 1
,

where these data are subject to the usual coherence axioms for
\alpha
,
\lambda
and
\rho
.
This amounts to the following:

•

monoidal structures
(\boxtimes_{0},I_{0})
and
(\boxtimes_{1},I_{1})
on the categories
\mathbb{C}_{0}
and
\mathbb{C}_{1}
;

•

strict monoidality of
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathbb{C}_{0}
;

•

globular 2-morphisms

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}\boxtimes C_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}\boxtimes C_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(y_{1}\circ x_{1})\boxtimes(y_{2}\circ x_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\xi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{1}\boxtimes x_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{1}\boxtimes y_{2}}

and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}\mathrlap{,}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\upsilon}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\delta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{1}}

and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}\mathrlap{,}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\iota}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{I_{0}}}

subject to axioms that make
\boxtimes
and
I
into oplax double functors,
and make the associativity and unitality constraints of
\boxtimes_{0}
and

\boxtimes_{1}
into the components of vertical transformations
\alpha
,

\lambda
and
\rho
.

If
\mathbb{C}
has an oplax monoidal structure
(\boxtimes,I)
, then it is
clear that the monoidal structure on
\mathbb{C}_{1}
restricts back to a
monoidal structure on the subcategory
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
: but due to the
oplaxity, this monoidal structure will
not
lift to
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
.
However, we can obtain a partial
lifting of
\boxtimes
by assuming that the oplax monoidal structure is

normal
in the following sense (cf.
[
GGV24
, Definition 4.3]
):

Definition 2.5.2
.

An oplax monoidal double category
\mathbb{C}
is said to be
normal
if:

(1)

I\colon\mathbf{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
is a (pseudo) double functor;

(2)

for all objects
A_{1},A_{2}\in\mathbb{C}
, the following restricted oplax double functors are (pseudo) double functors:

\displaystyle A_{1}\boxtimes({\mathord{\text{--}}})

\displaystyle\colon\mathbb{C}\cong\mathbf{1}\times\mathbb{C}\xrightarrow{A_{1}\times\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}\xrightarrow{\boxtimes}\mathbb{C}

\displaystyle\text{and}\qquad({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes A_{2}

\displaystyle\colon\mathbb{C}\cong\mathbb{C}\times\mathbf{1}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{C}\times A_{2}}\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}\xrightarrow{\boxtimes}\mathbb{C}\mathrlap{.}

Said another way, all three
2
-morphisms
\delta
,
\iota
and
\upsilon

from
2.5.1
are invertible, while each
\xi
for which

x_{1}=y_{1}=\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}
or
x_{2}=y_{2}=\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}}
is also
invertible.

.

If the
\mathcal{V}
of our running example is

(or

{

given by

(x\boxtimes y)\bigl[(a^{\prime},b^{\prime});(a,b)\bigr]=x[a^{\prime};a]\otimes y[b^{\prime};b]\hbox to0.0pt{ ;\hss}

the extension of this to
2
-morphisms is evident and left to the
reader. In this case, it is obvious that there are invertible cells

\nu
,
\iota
and
\delta
as in
2.5.1
, and we
can define
\xi
using the symmetry isomorphisms of
\mathcal{V}
. In
this case, every component of
\xi
is invertible, so that we have
not just a normal oplax monoidal double category, but a (pseudo)
monoidal double category: see, for instance,

[
ASV24
, Examples 3.2.2]
.

A more general situation is that
\mathcal{V}
is a (non-symmetric,
non-braided) normal duoidal category
(\mathcal{V},\circ,I,\boxtimes,J)

wherein
\circ
distributives over coproducts. Then we can use the

\circ
-monoidal structure to form
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
, and can use the

\boxtimes
-monoidal structure to define a normal oplax monoidal
structure on
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
; so now

(x\boxtimes y)\bigl[(a^{\prime},b^{\prime});(a,b)\bigr]=x[a^{\prime};a]\boxtimes y[b^{\prime};b]
. In this
case, the maps
\xi
are defined using the
interchangers of the duoidal category
\mathcal{V}
, which are not always
invertible, and so we get a normal oplax monoidal double category
which is
not
(pseudo) monoidal.

For the purposes of our running example, it will be clearer if we
focus on the more familiar case of a symmetric monoidal
\mathcal{V}
,
despite it not illustrating the full generality of our results;
however, we will also comment on the normal duoidal case where it
may add further insight.

Recall from Remark
2.2.3
that
\Delta_{A}
is
our notation for
(A,\mathrm{id}_{A})
, seen as an object
of
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
.

Lemma 2.5.4
.

Assume the oplax monoidal structure
(\boxtimes,I)
on the double category

\mathbb{C}
is normal. Then for each
A\in\mathbb{C}
, the functor
({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes B\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
lifts to a
functor
({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\colon\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
. Similarly, there is a functor
\Delta_{A}\boxtimes({\mathord{\text{--}}})\colon\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
.

In our running example, the functor
({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes\Delta_{B}
sends a

\mathcal{V}
-category
\mathcal{A}
to the coproduct of
B
copies of
\mathcal{A}
; thus, it yields the
\mathcal{V}
-category with object-set
A\times B
and hom-object
from
(a,b)
to
(a^{\prime},b^{\prime})
given by
\mathcal{A}(a,a^{\prime})
if
b=b^{\prime}
and
0

otherwise.

Proof.

Since

({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes B\colon\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
is a

pseudo
double functor by Definition
2.5.2
2
,
it sends monads to monads, e.g.
[
Vas19
, Prop. 3.12]
. Thus, if

(A,a)
is a monad in
\mathbb{C}
, then we make
(A,a)\boxtimes\Delta_{B}=(A\boxtimes B,a\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B})
into a monad via the maps

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{A\boxtimes B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\upsilon^{-1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{A}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\eta\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B}}

where

is a unit coherence constraint for the double

.
∎

We will also need a notion of
closedness
for oplax monoidal
double categories. For (pseudo) monoidal double categories, this was
given in
[
ASV24
, Definition 3.2.9]
, and the below is the
evident adaptation of this to the oplax monoidal case.

Definition 2.5.5
.

An oplax monoidal double category
(\mathbb{C},\boxtimes,I)
is said to be

left closed
if
the monoidal categories
(\mathbb{C}_{0},\boxtimes_{0},I_{0})
and
(\mathbb{C}_{1},\boxtimes_{1},I_{1})
admit left closures

({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes_{0}B\dashv\langle B,{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle_{0}\qquad\text{and}\qquad({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes_{1}y\dashv\langle y,{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle_{1}

which are strictly preserved by source and target; i.e., we have a serially commuting diagram

(13)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{1}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbb{C}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{0}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbb{C}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle{\mathord{\text{--}}},{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{t}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{t}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle{\mathord{\text{--}}},{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle_{0}}

for which
\mathfrak{s}
and
\mathfrak{t}
furthermore send the
evaluation maps
\mathsf{ev}_{y,z}\colon\langle y,z\rangle_{1}\boxtimes_{1}y\rightarrow z
in

\mathbb{C}_{1}
to the corresponding evaluation maps

\mathsf{ev}_{\mathfrak{s}(y),\mathfrak{s}(z)}
and
\mathsf{ev}_{\mathfrak{t}(y),\mathfrak{t}(z)}
in
\mathbb{C}_{0}
.

.

defined as follows; here,

denotes the internal hom in

.

\langle y,z\rangle[g^{\prime};g]\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\prod_{b\in B,b^{\prime}\in B^{\prime}}\Big[y[b^{\prime};b],\ z\big[g^{\prime}(b^{\prime});g(b)\big]\Big]\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

Note that all of this continues to work for a normal duoidal
(\mathcal{V},\circ,I,\boxtimes,J)
—so long as we now assume that the
\boxtimes
-tensor product is left closed.

When the oplax monoidal structure on
\mathbb{C}
is closed, the internal
hom
\langle{\mathord{\text{--}}},{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle
of
\mathbb{C}_{1}
clearly restricts
back to one on the subcategory
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
; but once again, this internal
hom does
not
lift to
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
. Now, as explained
in
[
ASV24
, Theorem 3.2.7]
, the oplax double
functoriality constraints of
\boxtimes
transport under the mates
correspondence to
lax
double functoriality constraints on the
morphism of
\mathsf{Cat}
-graphs
Eq.

13
. In other
words, we have a lax “hom double functor”

\langle{\mathord{\text{--}}},{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle\colon\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
, and using this, we are able to obtain a
partial
lifting of the
internal hom to monads, by analogy with

2.5.4
.

Lemma 2.5.7
.

Let
(\mathbb{C},\boxtimes,I)
be an oplax monoidal double category.

(1)

If

(\mathbb{C},\boxtimes,I)
is closed, then, for every
B\in\mathbb{C}
, the functor

\langle B,{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
lifts to
a functor
\langle\Delta_{B},{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle\colon\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
.

(2)

If
(\mathbb{C},\boxtimes,I)
is also normal, then the
adjunction

({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes B\dashv\langle B,{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
lifts to an adjunction

({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\dashv\langle\Delta_{B},{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle\colon\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

Running Example 2.5.8
.

In the case of
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
, the functor
\langle\Delta_{B},{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle
sends a
\mathcal{V}
-category
\mathcal{C}
to the
\mathcal{V}
-category
\mathcal{C}^{B}
, whose objects are
B
-indexed families of objects of
\mathcal{C}
, and whose homs are given by
\mathcal{C}^{B}(\vec{x},\vec{y})=\prod_{b\in B}\mathcal{C}(x_{b},y_{b})
.

Proof.

For (i), composing the lax double functor

\langle{\mathord{\text{--}}},{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle\colon\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
with the (pseudo) double functor
\mathbf{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}

picking out the object
B
yields a lax double functor

\langle B,{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle\colon\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
, which thus sends
monads to monads. More explicitly, if
(C,c)
is a monad in
\mathbb{C}
,
then we make

\langle\Delta_{B},(C,c)\rangle=\bigl(\langle B,C\rangle,\langle\mathrm{id}_{B},c\rangle\bigr)
into a monad via the transposes of the following

2
-morphisms under the adjunction

({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B}\dashv\langle\mathrm{id}_{B},{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{1}
:

(14)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle B,C\rangle\boxtimes B}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle B,C\rangle\boxtimes B}

For (ii), note that the (pseudo) double functor
({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes B\colon\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
and
the lax double functor
\langle B,{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle\colon\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
are adjoint in the
2
-category of double categories, lax
double functors and vertical transformations. The process of taking
monads is a
2
-functor from this
2
-category to the
2
-category
of categories, and so we have
({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\dashv\boxtimes{\Delta_{B},{\mathord{\text{--}}}}
as desired.
∎

Finally in this section, we define what it means for an oplax monoidal
double category to be
braided
and

symmetric
—generalising, for example,

[
HS19
]
to our more general oplax monoidal context.

Definition 2.5.9
.

Let
(\mathbb{C},\boxtimes,I)
be an oplax monoidal double category. A

braiding
on
\mathbb{C}
is an invertible vertical transformation

\beta\colon\boxtimes\Rightarrow\boxtimes\circ(\pi_{2},\pi_{1})
,
where
(\pi_{2},\pi_{1})\colon\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}
is the
double functor which interchanges its two arguments, satisfying the usual axioms.
More elementarily, this amounts to:

•

braidings for the monoidal structures on the categories
\mathbb{C}_{0}
and
\mathbb{C}_{1}
;

•

preservation of the braiding by the strict monoidal functors

\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathbb{C}_{0}
,
which is to say that the components of the braiding for
\mathbb{C}_{1}

have those for
\mathbb{C}_{0}
as their vertical components:

(15)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}\boxtimes A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}\boxtimes B_{1};}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta_{A_{1},A_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{1}\boxtimes x_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\beta_{x_{1},x_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta_{B_{1},B_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{2}\boxtimes x_{1}}

We say that the braiding
\beta
is a
symmetry
when

\beta^{-1}=\beta\circ(\pi_{2},\pi_{1})
; equivalently, we may ask
that the braided monoidal structures on
\mathbb{C}_{0}
and
\mathbb{C}_{1}
are
symmetric.

Running Example 2.5.10
.

If
\mathcal{V}
is a braided or symmetric monoidal category, then
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
will be braided or symmetric as a normal oplax double category, with the braiding maps given by those of
\mathsf{Set}
at the vertical level, and those of
\mathcal{V}
at the horizontal level. Of course, the situation here is slightly degenerate; for the more general case of a normal duoidal base
(\mathcal{V},\circ,I,\boxtimes,J)
, the relevant assumption is that the
\boxtimes
-tensor product is braided or symmetric as appropriate.

2.6.
Overview of assumptions

In the following sections, we will work with
a symmetric normal oplax monoidal closed double category, as per
2.5.1
,
2.5.2
,
2.5.5
and
2.5.9
.
We list the key assumptions on the (underlying) double category that we use for our
main theorems in
Table

2
for the convenience of the readers. These
will be assumed progressively, so as to highlight where they are
needed.

Table 2.
List of assumptions.

(1)

\mathbb{C}
is fibrant.

(2)

Each
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
has finite coproducts.

(3)

\mathbb{C}_{0}
has equalisers.

(4)

\mathbb{C}
has
1
-tabulators.

(5)

Each
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
has a left adjoint.

(6)

Each
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
has coequalisers.

(7)

\mathbb{C}
has local equalisers.

(8)

\mathbb{C}
has stable local reflexive coequalisers.

In
Section

6
we will show that, for a symmetric monoidal category
\mathcal{V}
satisfying appropriate assumptions,
the double categories
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
of
\mathcal{V}
-matrices, and
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
of categorical symmetric sequences,
admit a symmetric oplax monoidal closed structure and satisfy the assumptions listed in
Table

2
. This will enable us to apply our theory and obtain results about the
double categories
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
and
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{MultProf}_{\mathcal{V}}
of profunctors and symmetric multiprofunctors, respectively.

3.
The non-commuting tensor product of monads

In this section, we begin work towards our first main result, establishing the existence of a commuting monoidal structure on the category
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
of monads in a suitable oplax monoidal double category. This goal will only be achieved in the next section; in the present one, we instead establish the existence of a “non-commuting” monoidal structure on
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
which generalises of the so-called “funny tensor product” of categories. While this monoidal structure has some independent interest, for us it is largely a stepping-stone towards the commuting tensor product. This is true at a technical level—since the commuting monoidal structure will be constructed using the non-commuting one—but also at an expositional level. Indeed, the proof strategy in both sections is deliberately the same, so that the case of the non-commuting structure may serve as a useful warm-up to the reader for the more involved commuting one.

The main obstacle we face is that of constructing the associativity and unit coherences for the commuting tensor product. Rather than attempt this directly, we instead choose to make
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
into the underlying category of a symmetric multicategory, and to show that this is
representable
; then, by general arguments,
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
becomes a symmetric monoidal category under the tensor product representing these multimorphisms. Even this is not entirely straightforward: the problematic aspect is that representability must be verified with parameters. Thus, again, we take a different approach: we verify a weaker form of representability without parameters, which we term
pre-representability
, and then show that our multicategory is
closed
. By an argument familiar from categorical logic and proof theory, this allows us to bootstrap representability with parameters from that without and so, finally, obtain the desired symmetric monoidal structure—which, in addition, will now also be known to be closed.

As stated, the above proof strategy will be deployed twice, once for the non-commuting and once for the commuting case, with the differentiating factor being the choice of multicategory structure imposed on
monads. For the non-commuting case, it is not particularly hard to proceed in a much more direct way, and indeed, we sketch such an approach in
3.3.12
. However, for the reasons adumbrated above, we prefer to mirror precisely the structure of the proof for the commuting case: as we now begin to do.

3.1.
The multicategory of monads and multimorphisms

Let
(\mathbb{C},\boxtimes,I)
be a symmetric normal oplax monoidal double category, as in
2.5.1
,
2.5.2
and
2.5.9
. In this section, we will make
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
into the underlying category of a symmetric multicategory
\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
which, in the case where
\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathsf{Set}}
, will have as its
n
-ary multimorphisms the functors in
n
variables in the sense described in the introduction.

In order to ease the notational burden, we introduce some
conventions for working with indices.

Notation 3.1.1
.

Given a list of objects
A_{i},A_{i+1},\dots,A_{j\textrm{-}1},A_{j}
in

\mathbb{C}_{0}
, we may write:

•

A_{[i,j]}
as an abbreviation for

A_{i}\boxtimes A_{i+1}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes A_{j\textrm{-}1}\boxtimes A_{j}
;

•

\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}1_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}1_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}1_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}1_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[i,j]}
as an abbreviation for

1_{A_{i}}\boxtimes\dots\boxtimes 1_{A_{j}}
;

•

\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\mathrm{id}_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\mathrm{id}_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\mathrm{id}_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\mathrm{id}_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[i,j]}
as an abbreviation for

\mathrm{id}_{A_{i}}\boxtimes\dots\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{j}}
;

•

\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}1_{\mathrm{id}_{A}}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}1_{\mathrm{id}_{A}}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}1_{\mathrm{id}_{A}}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}1_{\mathrm{id}_{A}}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[i,j]}
as an abbreviation for

1_{\mathrm{id}_{A_{i}}}\boxtimes\dots\boxtimes 1_{\mathrm{id}_{A_{j}}}
;

•

\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[i,j]}
as an abbreviation for

\Delta_{A_{i}}\boxtimes\dots\boxtimes\Delta_{A_{j}}
;

and so on.

For the next definition, recall from
2.2.3
that
\Delta_{A}
denotes the discrete monad on an object
A\in\mathbb{C}_{0}
and that, by
2.5.4
, if
(B,b)
is a monad then
\Delta_{A}\boxtimes(B,b)=(A\boxtimes B,\mathrm{id}_{A}\boxtimes b)
is also a monad (and dually).

Definition 3.1.2
.

Let
(A_{1},a_{1}),\ldots,(A_{n},a_{n}),(B,b)
be monads in
\mathbb{C}
. A
monad multimorphism

(f,\vec{\phi})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\ldots,(A_{n},a_{n})\to(B,b)

is a vertical map
f\colon A_{1}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes A_{n}\to B
together
with 2-morphisms

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{[1,n]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{[1,n]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\displaystyle($}}}}\mathrm{id}_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\textstyle($}}}}\mathrm{id}_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\scriptstyle($}}}}\mathrm{id}_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\mathrm{id}_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[1,i\textrm{-}1]}\boxtimes a_{i}\boxtimes\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\displaystyle($}}}}\mathrm{id}_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\textstyle($}}}}\mathrm{id}_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\scriptstyle($}}}}\mathrm{id}_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\mathrm{id}_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[i{+}1,n]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\phi_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}

for every
1\leq i\leq n
, that provide the data for monad
maps

(16)

(f,\phi_{i})\colon\Delta_{A_{1}}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\Delta_{A_{i-1}}\boxtimes\,(A_{i},a_{i})\,\boxtimes\Delta_{A_{i+1}}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\Delta_{A_{n}}\rightarrow(B,b)\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

In particular, a unary monad multimorphism is the same as a monad
morphism
(A,a)\rightarrow(B,b)
; while a nullary monad
multimorphism is the same as a map
I\rightarrow B
in
\mathbb{C}_{0}
.

Running Example 3.1.3
.

In the case of
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
, a binary monad multimorphism
(f,\phi,\psi)\colon(A,a),(B,b)\rightarrow(C,c)
is the same as a
\mathcal{V}
-functor of two variables
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
(or
\mathcal{V}
-sesquifunctor) in the sense of the introduction. Indeed:

•

The function
f\colon A\times B\rightarrow C
encodes an assignment on objects
(a,b)\mapsto F(a,b)
;

•

The monad morphism
(f,\phi)\colon(A,a)\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\rightarrow(C,c)
is equally a
\mathcal{V}
-functor
\sum_{b\in B}\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
with action
f
on objects, so equally a family of
\mathcal{V}
-functors
(F({\mathord{\text{--}}},b)\colon\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{C})_{a\in A}
satisfying
F({\mathord{\text{--}}},b)(a)=F(a,b)
;

•

Likewise,
(f,\psi)\colon\Delta_{A}\boxtimes(B,b)\rightarrow(C,c)
is equally a family of
\mathcal{V}
-functors
(F(a,{\mathord{\text{--}}})\colon\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathcal{C})_{b\in B}
satisfying
F(a,{\mathord{\text{--}}})(b)=F(a,b)
.

Thus, a binary monad multimorphism comprises
\mathcal{V}
-functors
(F({\mathord{\text{--}}},b)\colon\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{C})_{a\in A}
and
(F({\mathord{\text{--}}},b)\colon\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{C})_{a\in A}
satisfying
F(a,{\mathord{\text{--}}})(b)=F({\mathord{\text{--}}},b)(a)
for all
a,b
: which is precisely a functor of two variables as in the introduction. The
n
-ary case is similar: for example, a ternary monad multimorphism corresponds to a functor of three variables
F\colon\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
involving families of
\mathcal{V}
-functors
F(a,b,{\mathord{\text{--}}})
and
F({\mathord{\text{--}}},b,c)
and
F(a,{\mathord{\text{--}}},c)
which agree on objects in the evident way.

For the definition of a symmetric multicategory, see for example
[
Lei04
,
Yau16
]
. Below we use the ‘circle-
i
’ or ‘pseudo-operad’ formulation of the definition, which is equivalent to the standard one (see e.g.
[
Yau16
, Thm. 16.4.1]
).

Proposition 3.1.4
.

There is a symmetric multicategory
\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
with monad as
objects and monad multimorphisms as maps.

Proof.

For every monad
(A,a)
, the (unary) identity multimorphism is given
by the identity monad map
(1_{A},\mathrm{id}_{a})\colon(A,a)\to(A,a)
.
Moreover, given monad multimorphisms

(g,\vec{\theta})\colon(B_{1},b_{1}),\ldots,(B_{m},b_{m})\to(C,c)\qquad\text{and}\qquad(f,\vec{\phi})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\ldots,(A_{n},a_{n})\to(B_{i},b_{i}),

the composite
(g,\vec{\theta})\circ_{i}(f,\vec{\phi})
is the monad multimorphism

(B_{1},b_{1}),\ldots,(B_{i\textrm{-}1},b_{i\textrm{-}1}),(A_{1},a_{1}),\ldots(A_{n},a_{n}),(B_{i+1},b_{i+1}),\ldots,(B_{m},b_{m})\to(C,c)

defined as follows. The vertical map is formed as

B_{[1,i\textrm{-}1]}\boxtimes A_{[1,n]}\boxtimes B_{[i+1,m]}\xrightarrow{\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}1_{B}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}1_{B}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}1_{B}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}1_{B}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[1,i\textrm{-}1]}\boxtimes\,f\,\boxtimes\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}1_{B}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}1_{B}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}1_{B}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}1_{B}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[i+1,m]}}B_{[1,i\textrm{-}1]}\boxtimes B_{i}\boxtimes B_{[i+1,m]}\xrightarrow{\ \ g\ \ }C

while the 2-morphisms providing the monad map components split up into
two cases. The first case involves one of the
b_{k}
-monads in the
domain; we illustrate with the case
k=1
, but there are analogous
diagrams for
k=2,\dots,i-1,i+1,\dots,m
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{[1,i\textrm{-}1]}\boxtimes A_{[1,n]}\boxtimes B_{[i+1,m]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{[1,i\textrm{-}1]}\boxtimes A_{[1,n]}\boxtimes B_{[i+1,m]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{[1,m]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{[1,m]}}
