Finally, for any multimap
(f,\vec{\phi})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\ldots,(A_{n},a_{n})\to(B,b)
and any permutation
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
, the action of
\sigma
on
(f,\vec{\varphi})
yields the monad multimorphism

(A_{\sigma(1)},a_{\sigma(1)}),\ldots,(A_{\sigma(n)},a_{\sigma(n)})\to(B,b)

that consists of the vertical map
A_{\sigma(1)}\boxtimes\ldots\boxtimes A_{\sigma(n)}\xrightarrow{\beta_{\sigma}}A_{1}\boxtimes\ldots\boxtimes A_{n}\xrightarrow{f}B
—where here and below,
\beta_{\sigma}
represents appropriate applications of the symmetry of
\mathbb{C}
as in
Eq.

15
—and the monad map components

It can now be verified that these data form monad maps, due to the axioms that
\beta_{\sigma}
satisfies, and that this assignment constitutes an action of the symmetric group
\mathfrak{S}_{n}
on
n
-ary monad multimorphisms. Furthermore, one can verify the associativity, unitality and equivariance axioms (found e.g. in
[
Yau16
, Def. 16.2.1]
), thus showing that monads and monad multimorphisms form a symmetric multicategory.

To make this even more concrete, we continue our:

Running Example 3.1.5
.

Given a
\mathcal{V}
-functor of three variables
G\colon\mathcal{B}_{1},\mathcal{B}_{2},\mathcal{B}_{3}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
and a
\mathcal{V}
-functor of two variables
F\colon\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{2}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}_{2}
, the composite
G\circ_{2}F
is the
\mathcal{V}
-functor of four variables
\mathcal{B}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{2},\mathcal{B}_{3}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
with

\displaystyle(G\circ F)({\mathord{\text{--}}},a_{1},a_{2},b_{3})

\displaystyle=G({\mathord{\text{--}}},F(a_{1},a_{2}),b_{3})

\displaystyle(G\circ F)(b_{1},{\mathord{\text{--}}},a_{2},b_{3})

\displaystyle=G(b_{1},F({\mathord{\text{--}}},a_{2}),b_{3})

\displaystyle(G\circ F)(b_{1},a_{1},{\mathord{\text{--}}},b_{3})

\displaystyle=G(b_{1},F(a_{1},{\mathord{\text{--}}}),b_{3})

\displaystyle(G\circ F)(b_{1},a_{1},a_{2},{\mathord{\text{--}}})

\displaystyle=G(b_{1},F(a_{1},a_{2}),{\mathord{\text{--}}})\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

3.2.
Pre-representability of
\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})

We now start building towards
3.3.10
, which
proves that the symmetric multicategory
\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
of monads in

\mathbb{C}
is
representable
in the sense of

[
Her00
]
.

Definition 3.2.1
.

A symmetric multicategory

\mathcal{M}
is
representable
if for every
n
-tuple of objects

A_{1}\dots,A_{n}
, there is an object
A_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes A_{n}

and multimorphism

A_{1},\dots,A_{n}\rightarrow A_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes A_{n}
which is

universal
, in the sense that composition with it induces
bijections of multimorphism-sets

(17)

\begin{array}[]{@{\,\,}r@{\,}l@{\ }l@{\ }c@{\ }l@{\ }l@{\,\,}}f\colon&Z_{1},\dots,Z_{k},&A_{1},\ \,\dots,\,\ A_{n},&Z_{k+1},\dots,Z_{n}&\longrightarrow&C\\
\vskip 2.0pt\cr\hline\cr\vskip 2.5pt\cr f^{\sharp}\colon&Z_{1},\dots,Z_{k},&A_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes A_{n},&Z_{k+1},\dots,Z_{n}&\longrightarrow&C\end{array}

for all codomains
C
and parameters
Z_{1},\dots,Z_{n}
.

As explained in the introduction to this section, the presence of the
parameters complicates the task of checking universality. What is
easier is to establish the existence of
pre-universal

morphisms, which exhibit the bijections
Eq.

17

only when there are no parameters
Z_{i}
4
4

4

Note that universal
and pre-universal morphisms are referred to as strong universal and
universal, respectively, in
[
Her00
]
; our nomenclature
follows, e.g.
[
Lei04
, Def. 3.3.2]
.
. We will do this for

\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
, and deduce their full universality in the next section
by showing that
\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
is a
closed
multicategory.

In fact, in the presence of a closed structure, it suffices for
representability that we have
binary
and
nullary

pre-universal morphisms; as such, it will be convenient for us to
adopt the—perhaps slightly misleading—term

pre-representable
for a multicategory in which just these
pre-universal morphisms exist.

In order to establish the pre-representability of
\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
, we make the following assumptions.

Assumption I
.

The double category
\mathbb{C}
is fibrant, as in
2.1.3
.

Assumption II
.

Each category
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
has finite coproducts.

In this context, the codomain of the pre-universal binary multimorphism
(A,a),(B,b)\rightarrow(A,a)\mathbin{\Box}(B,b)
, which is the desired
non-commuting tensor product
of
(A,a)
and
(B,b)
, will be the monad
a\mathbin{\Box}b
on the object
A\boxtimes B
obtained as the coproduct

(18)

(A\boxtimes B,a\mathbin{\Box}b)=(A,a)\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\,+\,\Delta_{A}\boxtimes(B,b)

in
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A\boxtimes B}(\mathbb{C})

Proposition 3.2.2
.

The symmetric multicategory
\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
is pre-representable.

Proof.

First of all, since nullary monad multimorphisms into
(B,b)
are
the same as maps
f\colon I\rightarrow B
in
\mathbb{C}_{0}
, and these
are in turn the same as monad morphisms

\Delta_{I}\rightarrow(B,b)
, we see that there is a pre-universal
nullary map given by
1_{I}\colon\ \longrightarrow\Delta_{I}
.

As for the binary case, let
(A,a),(B,b)\in\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
. We show that there is a pre-universal binary multimorphism

(20)

(1_{A\boxtimes B},\iota_{1},\iota_{2})\colon(A,a),(B,b)\rightarrow(A\boxtimes B,a\mathbin{\Box}b)

where
(A,a)\mathbin{\Box}(B,b)
is defined as in
Eq.

18
, and
\iota_{1}
and
\iota_{2}
are the coproduct inclusions in the fibre
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})_{A\boxtimes B}
, as in (
19
).
For this, we must show that composition with (
20
) induces for each monad
(C,c)
a bijection

(21)

\begin{split}(A,a),(B,b)&\to(C,c)\qquad\textrm{in }\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})\\
\vskip 3.0pt plus 1.0pt minus 1.0pt\cr\hline\cr\vskip 3.0pt plus 1.0pt minus 1.0pt\cr(A\boxtimes B,a\mathbin{\Box}b)&\to(C,c)\qquad\textrm{in }\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\end{split}

or in other words, that each binary monad multimorphism

(f,\phi,\psi)\colon(A,a),(B,b)\to(C,c)
factors uniquely through

(1,\iota_{1},\iota_{2})
. Now, given such an
(f,\phi,\psi)
, we have a
square in
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Delta_{A\boxtimes B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Delta_{A}\boxtimes(B,b)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A,a)\boxtimes\Delta_{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(C,c)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\eta_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\eta_{1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f,\psi)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f,\phi)}

which evidently commutes at the level of objects and so, by the
adjointness of
\Delta_{({\mathord{\text{--}}})}
to the forgetful functor

\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
, commutes simpliciter.
Since (
19
) is a pushout, we induce a monad map

(A\boxtimes B,a\mathbin{\Box}b)\rightarrow(C,c)
which is unique such that it
precomposes with
(1,\iota_{1})
, respectively
(1,\iota_{2})
, to yield

(f,\phi)
, respectively
(f,\psi)
. Clearly, this is the desired
unique factorisation of
(f,\phi,\psi)
through
(1,\iota_{1},\iota_{2})
.
∎

Running Example 3.2.3
.

\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
is always fibrant; and if
\mathcal{V}
has colimits preserved by tensor in each variable, then we will also have finite coproducts in each
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
. Indeed, given monads
(A,a_{1})
and
(A,a_{2})
, their coproduct is found by first forming the free monad on
(A,a_{1}\circ a_{2})
, and then taking a suitable coequaliser, formed in
\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
in the first instance, but after the fact lifting to
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
. In the case of
\mathcal{V}=\mathsf{Set}
, this can be described as the coequaliser which forces the equalities

\displaystyle\cdots x_{2k-2}\xrightarrow{f_{k}}x_{2k-1}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}x_{2k}\xrightarrow{f_{k+1}}x_{2k+1}\xrightarrow{g_{k+1}}x_{2k+2}\cdots\ \

\displaystyle=\ \ \cdots x_{2k-2}\xrightarrow{f_{k+1}f_{k}}x_{2k+1}\xrightarrow{g_{k+1}}x_{2k+2}\cdots

\displaystyle\text{and }\cdots x_{2k-2}\xrightarrow{f_{k}}x_{2k-1}\xrightarrow{g_{k}}x_{2k}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}x_{2k+1}\xrightarrow{g_{k+1}}x_{2k+2}\cdots\ \

\displaystyle=\ \ \cdots x_{2k-2}\xrightarrow{f_{k}}x_{2k+1}\xrightarrow{g_{k+1}g_{k}}x_{2k+2}\cdots\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

The induced non-commuting tensor product
\mathbin{\Box}
is, in the case
\mathcal{V}=\mathsf{Set}
, the so-called
funny tensor product
; for an explicit description, see, e.g.,
[
Web13
, §2]
.

There is no obstacle to extending the argument of the previous
proposition to
n
-ary pre-universal maps; for example,
the ternary case involves a coproduct

(A,a)\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\boxtimes\Delta_{C}+\Delta_{A}\boxtimes(B,b)\boxtimes\Delta_{C}+\Delta_{A}\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\boxtimes(C,c)
in
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A\boxtimes B\boxtimes C}(\mathbb{C})
.
However, as noted above, doing so is supererogatory in the presence of
closed structure on our multicategory—as we will now see.

3.3.
Closure and representability of
\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})

Let us recall (cf.
[
Lam69
,
Man12
]
):

Definition 3.3.1
.

A symmetric multicategory
\mathcal{M}

is
closed
if, for every
B,C\in\mathcal{M}
, there is an object

[B,C]\in\mathcal{M}
and a binary multimorphism
\mathsf{ev}\colon[B,C],B\rightarrow C
, composition with which induces bijections
between multimorphism-sets

\begin{array}[]{@{\,\,}r@{\,}l@{\ }c@{\ }l@{\,\,}}f\colon&A_{1},\dots,A_{n},B&\longrightarrow&C\\
\vskip 2.0pt\cr\hline\cr\vskip 2.5pt\cr\bar{f}\colon&A_{1},\dots,A_{n}&\longrightarrow&[B,C]\mathrlap{.}\end{array}

The relevance of this for us is the following result, which appears to
be folklore in this generality—though it can be deduced as a special
case of
[
BL18
, Prop. 4.8]
.

Proposition 3.3.2
.

If a multicategory
\mathcal{M}

is pre-representable and closed, then it is representable.

Proof.

Since
\mathcal{M}
is pre-representable, it has pre-universal binary
morphisms
u_{A,B}\colon A,B\rightarrow A\otimes B
for all
objects
A,B
. We first show that these are universal. Indeed,
given a multimorphism as on the first line in

\begin{array}[]{@{\,\,}r@{\,}l@{\ }l@{\ }c@{\ }l@{\ }l@{\,\,}}f\colon&Z_{1},\dots,Z_{k},&A,\ B,&Z_{k+1},\dots,Z_{n}&\longrightarrow&C\\
\vskip 2.0pt\cr\hline\cr\vskip 2.5pt\cr\bar{f}\colon&&A,\ B&&\longrightarrow&[Z_{1},[Z_{2},\dots[Z_{n},C]\cdots]\\
\vskip 2.0pt\cr\hline\cr\vskip 2.5pt\cr{\bar{f}}^{\sharp}\colon&&A\!\otimes\!B&&\longrightarrow&[Z_{1},[Z_{2},\dots[Z_{n},C]\cdots]\\
\vskip 2.0pt\cr\hline\cr\vskip 2.5pt\cr f^{\sharp}\colon&Z_{1},\dots,Z_{k},&A\!\otimes\!B,&Z_{k+1},\dots,Z_{n}&\longrightarrow&C\end{array}

we have a sequence of bijections as displayed. Here, from the first
to the second line, we use a combination of closedness and symmetry
isomorphisms; from the second to the third, we use
pre-representability; and from the third to the fourth, we again use
symmetry and closedness.

An identical argument shows that the nullary pre-universal morphism

\ \ \rightarrow I
is universal, so it remains to exhibit universal
arrows of other arities. This is formally the same as the standard argument
showing that nullary and binary products suffice for all finite
products; the key fact needed is that universal arrows are closed
under composition
[
Her00
, Proposition 8.5(1)]
.
∎

Thus, if we can show that the multicategory of monads and monad
multimorphisms is closed, then we can conclude that it is also
representable. This is not the only way to proceed, and is not
necessarily even the simplest way to proceed; however, when it comes
to the commuting tensor product in the following section, this
approach definitively
will
be the simplest one, and so we
match the form of the argument here. Of course, the closure is
also an interesting fact in its own right. We outline the other approach in

3.3.12
.

To prove closedness, we will assume that the symmetric normal
oplax monoidal structure of the double category
\mathbb{C}
is closed, as
in
2.5.5
, and make the following two further
assumptions on
\mathbb{C}
. Note that, even if we were to prove
representability of
\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
directly, some additional assumptions
would be needed; for example, it seems hard to avoid assuming that each
functor

\Delta_{A}\boxtimes({\mathord{\text{--}}})\colon\mathsf{Mnd}_{B}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{Mnd}_{A\boxtimes B}(\mathbb{C})

preserves finite coproducts. As such, it is not unreasonable that we
should make additional assumptions at this juncture.

Assumption III
.

The category
\mathbb{C}_{0}
has equalisers.

Assumption IV
.

The double category
\mathbb{C}
has
1
-tabulators, as in
2.4.5
.

To establish closedness, we will need three preparatory lemmas.

Lemma 3.3.3
.

The functor

(22)

\displaystyle\mathbb{C}_{0}\times\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})

\displaystyle\rightarrow\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})

\displaystyle(A,(B,y))

\displaystyle\mapsto(A,\mathrm{id}_{A})\boxtimes(B,y)

has a parametrised right adjoint

\underline{\smash{\mathsf{End}}}(\mathbb{C})\colon\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
.

It is easy to see that the above functor in fact gives a
monoidal action of
(\mathbb{C}_{0},\boxtimes)
on
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
. So by, for
example,
[
JK01
, Section 6]
, the parametrised right
adjoint
\underline{\smash{\mathsf{End}}}(\mathbb{C})
provides the hom-objects for an enrichment
of
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
in
(\mathbb{C}_{0},\boxtimes)
—whence our notation.

Proof.

For every
(B,y)\in\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
, we must exhibit a right adjoint namely

\underline{\smash{\mathsf{End}}}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((B,y),{\mathord{\text{--}}}\bigr)\colon\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
for
the functor

\mathrm{id}_{({\mathord{\text{--}}})}\boxtimes(B,y)\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
. Equivalently, we must show that for all
(B,y),(C,z)\in\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
,
the functor

\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})(\mathrm{id}_{({\mathord{\text{--}}})}\boxtimes y,z)\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}^{\mathrm{op}}\rightarrow\mathsf{Set}
is representable; the representing object will then be

\underline{\smash{\mathsf{End}}}(\mathbb{C})(y,z)
.

Note that the values of this
functor arise as the following equalisers in
\mathsf{Set}
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})(\mathrm{id}_{A}\boxtimes y,z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{1}\bigl((A,\mathrm{id}_{A})\boxtimes(B,y),(C,z)\bigr)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{0}(A\boxtimes B,C)\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{t}}

Thus, if we can prove representability of the functors

\mathbb{C}_{1}\bigl(\mathrm{id}_{({\mathord{\text{--}}})}\boxtimes(B,y),(C,z)\bigr)
and

\mathbb{C}_{0}({\mathord{\text{--}}}\boxtimes B,C)
, then
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})(\mathrm{id}_{({\mathord{\text{--}}})}\boxtimes y,z)
will
be a pointwise equaliser of representable functors

\mathbb{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathsf{Set}
and so also representable, given that
\mathbb{C}_{0}
by assumption has equalisers.

But
\mathbb{C}_{0}({\mathord{\text{--}}}\boxtimes B,C)
is representable since
(\mathbb{C}_{0},\boxtimes)
is closed, while
\mathbb{C}_{1}\bigl(\mathrm{id}_{({\mathord{\text{--}}})}\boxtimes(B,y),(C,z)\bigr)
is representable since

\mathbb{C}_{1}(\mathrm{id}_{({\mathord{\text{--}}})}\boxtimes y,z)\cong\mathbb{C}_{1}(\mathrm{id}_{({\mathord{\text{--}}})},\langle y,z\rangle)\cong\mathbb{C}_{0}({\mathord{\text{--}}},T\langle y,z\rangle)

using closedness of
(\mathbb{C}_{1},\boxtimes)
and 1-tabulators in
\mathbb{C}
.
Working this through, we find that the values of the parametrised
right adjoint to
Eq.

22
are given by the
following equalisers in
\mathbb{C}_{0}
:

Running Example 3.3.4
.

\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
always satisfies
III
and
IV
, and
is normal oplax monoidal closed so long as
\mathcal{V}
is monoidal
closed; we assume this henceforth. In this case,

\underline{\smash{\mathsf{End}}}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((B,y),(C,z)\bigr)
is simply the hom-set

\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((B,y),(C,z)\bigr)
, i.e., the set of
\mathcal{V}
-graph
morphisms from
(B,y)
to
(C,z)
.

Lemma 3.3.5
.

The lifting of the functor
Eq.

22

\displaystyle\mathbb{C}_{0}\times\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})

\displaystyle\rightarrow\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})

\displaystyle(A,(B,b))

\displaystyle\mapsto\Delta_{A}\boxtimes(B,b)

obtained via
2.5.4
, has a
parametrised right adjoint

\underline{\smash{\mathsf{Mnd}}}(\mathbb{C})\colon\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
.

Again, the values of
\underline{\smash{\mathsf{Mnd}}}(\mathbb{C})
provide the
hom-objects for an enrichment of
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
in
\mathbb{C}_{0}
.

Proof.

Note first that, for any monads
(B,b)
and
(C,c)
, the set

\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})(b,c)
is the limit of the diagram:

(23)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((B,b),(C,c)\bigr)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((B,b\circ b),(C,c)\bigr)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((B,\mathrm{id}_{B}),(C,c)\bigr)\mathrlap{,}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell_{2}}

where
\ell_{1}
and
r_{1}
, respectively
\ell_{2}
and
r_{2}
, send a map
(f,\varphi)
to
the left and right sides of the first, respectively the second, equality
in
Eq.

5
. Moreover, this limit can be
constructed from equalisers alone: we let
e
be an equaliser of

\ell_{1}
and
r_{1}
, and then form the equaliser of
\ell_{2}e
and

r_{2}e
.

Given
(B,b)
and
(C,c)\in\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
, we now show that

\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\bigl(\Delta_{{\mathord{\text{--}}}}\boxtimes(B,b),(C,c)\bigr)\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}^{\mathrm{op}}\rightarrow\mathsf{Set}
is representable. By the above, replacing
(B,b)
by
(A\boxtimes B,\mathrm{id}_{A}\boxtimes b)
, the value of this
functor at
A
is given by the limit:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((A\boxtimes B,\mathrm{id}_{A}\boxtimes b),(C,c)\bigr)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((A\boxtimes B,(\mathrm{id}_{A}\boxtimes b)\circ(\mathrm{id}_{A}\boxtimes b)),(C,c)\bigr)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((A\boxtimes B,\mathrm{id}_{A\boxtimes B}),(C,c)\bigr)\mathrlap{,}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell_{2}}

and so – arguing as before – it suffices to show
that each vertex of this diagram is representable as a functor of
its
A
-variable. For the top-left vertex, this follows immediately
from the preceding lemma; for the other two vertices, it follows
from the same lemma on noting that, by normality (
2.5.2
) of the oplax
monoidal structure
\boxtimes
, we have natural isomorphisms

\mathrm{id}_{A\boxtimes B}\cong\mathrm{id}_{A}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B}
and

(\mathrm{id}_{A}\boxtimes b)\circ(\mathrm{id}_{A}\boxtimes b)\cong\mathrm{id}_{A}\boxtimes(b\circ b)
.
Working this through, we find that
\underline{\smash{\mathsf{Mnd}}}(\mathbb{C})(b,c)
is the
limit of a diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\smash{\mathsf{End}}}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((B,b),(C,c)\bigr)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\smash{\mathsf{End}}}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((B,b\circ b),(C,c)\bigr)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\smash{\mathsf{End}}}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((B,\mathrm{id}_{B}),(C,c)\bigr)\hbox to0.0pt{ ,\hss}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\ell_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{r_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{r_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\ell_{2}}}

i.e., the “enhancement” of
Eq.

23
from a
diagram of sets to a diagram in
\mathbb{C}_{0}
.
∎

Running Example 3.3.6
.

In
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
, the object

\underline{\smash{\mathsf{Mnd}}}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((B,b),(C,c)\bigr)
is simply the set

\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((B,b),(C,c)\bigr)
, i.e., the set of

\mathcal{V}
-functors
\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
between the associated

\mathcal{V}
-categories of
(B,b)
and
(C,c)
.

Lemma 3.3.7
.

Let
(g,\gamma)\colon(B,b)\rightarrow(C,c)
be a map in
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
.
Assume that it is is cartesian with respect to the Grothendieck fibration

\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
. The following “enhanced
cartesianness” property with respect to the multicategory

\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
holds: any monad multimorphism
(gh,\vec{\phi})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n})\rightarrow(C,c)
factorises uniquely through
(g,\gamma)
. More compactly, for any monads
(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n})
, the
square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n});\,(B,b)\bigr)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n});\,(C,c)\bigr)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{0}(A_{1}\boxtimes\dots\boxtimes A_{n},B)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{0}(A_{1}\boxtimes\dots\boxtimes A_{n},C)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(g,\gamma)}\circ_{1}({\mathord{\text{--}}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g\circ({\mathord{\text{--}}})}

is a pullback, where the vertical arrows project onto the object-components.

Proof.

We must show there is a unique monad multimorphism
(h,\vec{\phi}^{\prime})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n})\rightarrow(B,b)
which factors

(gh,\vec{\phi})
through
(g,\gamma)
. But
the original monad multimorphism consists of monad maps

(24)

(gh,\phi_{i})\colon\Delta_{A_{1}}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes(A_{i},a_{i})\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\Delta_{A_{n}}\rightarrow(C,c)\hbox to0.0pt{ ,\hss}

so by the ordinary cartesianness of
(g,\gamma)
, there is a unique

(h,\phi^{\prime}_{i})\colon\Delta_{A_{1}}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes(A_{i},a_{i})\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\Delta_{A_{n}}\rightarrow(B,b)
in
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
which
factors
Eq.

24
through
(g,\gamma)
. It
is clear that the
(h,\vec{\phi}^{\prime})
so defined is the
unique monad multimorphism we seek.
∎

We now show that
the symmetric multicategory of monads and monad multimorphisms is closed.

Proposition 3.3.8
.

The symmetric multicategory
\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
is closed. More precisely,
for any monads
(B,b),(C,c)
, there exists a monad

\llbracket(B,b),(C,c)\rrbracket

and a binary
multimorphism

(25)

(e,\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2})\colon\llbracket(B,b),(C,c)\rrbracket,(B,b)\rightarrow(C,c)

composition with which induces bijections between multimorphism-sets

(26)

\begin{array}[]{r@{\,}l@{\ }c@{\ }l}(f,\phi_{1},\dots,\phi_{n},\psi)\colon&(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n}),(B,b)&\longrightarrow&(C,c)\\
\vskip 3.0pt\cr\hline\cr\vskip 3.0pt\cr(\bar{f},\bar{\phi}_{1},\dots,\bar{\phi}_{n})\colon&(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n})&\longrightarrow&\llbracket(B,b),(C,c)\rrbracket\end{array}

Notice that due to symmetry, we do not differentiate between left and right closedness.

Proof.

Consider first the case where
(B,b)
is the identity monad

\Delta_{B}
. In this case, it is easy to see that the final component
Eq.

16

of a multimorphism
Eq.

26

is forced to be the monad map

(27)

(f,\eta)\colon\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[1,n]}\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\xrightarrow{\cong}\Delta_{A_{1}\boxtimes\dots\boxtimes A_{n}}\xrightarrow{\Delta_{f}}\Delta_{C}\xrightarrow{(1_{C},\eta)}(C,c)\hbox to0.0pt{ ,\hss}

Thus, giving
Eq.

26
is the same
as giving a map

f\colon A_{[1,n]}\boxtimes B\rightarrow C
in
\mathbb{C}_{0}

and monad maps

(28)

(f,\phi_{i})\colon\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[1,i\textrm{-}1]}\boxtimes(A_{i},a_{i})\boxtimes\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[i+1,n]}\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\rightarrow(C,c)\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

Now, since
\mathbb{C}
is closed (
2.5.5
), we may transpose
f
to a map

\bar{f}\colon A_{[1,n]}\rightarrow\langle B,C\rangle

under the adjunction

({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes B\dashv\langle B,{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}\to\mathbb{C}_{0}
.
But since by
2.5.7
this adjunction
lifts to one

({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\dashv\langle\Delta_{B},{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle\colon\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
, we can also transpose
each
Eq.

28
to a
monad map

(\bar{f},{\bar{\phi}}_{i})\colon{\Delta_{A}}_{[1,i\textrm{-}1]}\boxtimes(A_{i},a_{i})\boxtimes{\Delta_{A}}_{[i+1,n]}\rightarrow\langle\Delta_{B},(C,c)\rangle\hbox to0.0pt{ ,\hss}

and so obtain a monad multimorphism

(\bar{f},\bar{\phi}_{1},\dots,\bar{\phi}_{n})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n})\rightarrow\langle\Delta_{B},(C,c)\rangle
. Thus, when

(B,b)=\Delta_{B}
, the desired internal hom is the monad

\langle\Delta_{B},(C,c)\rangle=(\langle B,C\rangle,\langle\mathrm{id}_{B},c\rangle)

equipped with the binary
multimorphism
Eq.

25
whose:

•

Object-component

e\colon\langle B,C\rangle\boxtimes B\rightarrow C

is the counit at
C
of the adjunction
({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes B\dashv\langle B,{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle
in
\mathbb{C}_{0}
;

•

First morphism-component

(e,\varepsilon_{1})\colon\langle\Delta_{B},(C,c)\rangle\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\rightarrow(C,c)
is the counit at
(C,c)
of the
lifted adjunction

({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\dashv\langle\Delta_{B},{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle
in
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
;

•

Second morphism-component

(e,\varepsilon_{2})\colon\Delta_{\langle B,C\rangle}\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\rightarrow(C,c)
is determined uniquely as in
Eq.

27
.

We now let
(B,b)
be a general monad and construct the internal hom

\llbracket(B,b),(C,c)\rrbracket
. Its underlying object
\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0}
in

\mathbb{C}_{0}
will be the the object
\underline{\smash{\mathsf{Mnd}}}(\mathbb{C})(b,c)\in\mathbb{C}_{0}

of
3.3.5
. As there, this object represents the functor

\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\bigl(\Delta_{({\mathord{\text{--}}})}\boxtimes(B,b),(C,c)\bigr)\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}^{\mathrm{op}}\rightarrow\mathsf{Set}
. On the other hand, the functor

\mathbb{C}_{0}({\mathord{\text{--}}}\boxtimes B,C)\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}^{\mathrm{op}}\rightarrow\mathsf{Set}
is
represented by
\langle B,C\rangle\in\mathbb{C}_{0}
since the latter is the internal hom of
\mathbb{C}
. Since, projecting to
object-components determines a natural transformation

\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\bigl(\Delta_{({\mathord{\text{--}}})}\boxtimes(B,b),(C,c)\bigr)\Rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}({\mathord{\text{--}}}\boxtimes B,C)\hbox to0.0pt{ ,\hss}

there is by the Yoneda lemma a map

(29)

i\colon\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0}\rightarrow\langle B,C\rangle

in
\mathbb{C}_{0}
with the property that factorisations of a map

\bar{f}\colon A\rightarrow\langle B,C\rangle
of
\mathbb{C}_{0}
through
i
are in
bijection with extensions of the exponential transpose

f\colon A\boxtimes B\rightarrow C
of
\bar{f}
to a monad morphism

(f,\psi)\colon\Delta_{A}\boxtimes(B,b)\rightarrow(C,c)\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

Since
\mathbb{C}
is fibrant, the forgetful functor

\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
is a fibration; thus, we may reindex the
monad
\langle\Delta_{B},(C,c)\rangle
on
\langle B,C\rangle

along
Eq.

29
to obtain a monad

\llbracket b,c\rrbracket
on
\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0}
and a cartesian
monad morphism

(30)

(i,\tilde{\imath})\colon(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)\rightarrow\langle\Delta_{B},(C,c)\rangle\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

We claim that
(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)
provides the
desired internal hom. For indeed, giving a monad
multimorphism
Eq.

26
is
equivalent to giving the following two things:

(1)

A monad
multimorphism of the following form, where
\tilde{f}
is uniquely determined by
f
as
in
Eq.

27
:

(f,\phi_{1},\dots,\phi_{n},\tilde{f})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n}),\Delta_{B}\rightarrow(C,c)\hbox to0.0pt{ ;\hss}

(2)

A monad morphism of the following form, where
3.1.1
is used:

(f,\psi)\colon\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[1,n]}\boxtimes(B,b)\rightarrow(C,c)\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

Now by the case proved earlier, giving the monad multimorphism in
(i) is equivalent to giving a multimorphism

(\bar{f},\bar{\phi}_{1},\dots,\bar{\phi}_{n})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n})\rightarrow\langle\Delta_{B},(C,c)\rangle
. On the
other hand, it follows from our characterisation of
i
that giving
the monad morphism in (ii) is equivalent to giving a factorisation
of
\bar{f}\colon A_{[1,n]}\rightarrow\langle B,C\rangle

through
i
in
\mathbb{C}_{0}
. But by
3.3.7
applied to the
cartesian monad map
Eq.

30
, giving
this factorisation of
\bar{f}
through
i
is equivalent to giving a
factorisation of
(\bar{f},\bar{\phi}_{1},\dots,\bar{\phi}_{n})

through
(i,\tilde{\imath})
in
\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
.

In this way, we have shown that there is a bijection between monad multimorphisms
Eq.

26
and ones

(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n})\rightarrow(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)
, so exhibiting
(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)
as the desired internal hom.
The evaluation map
Eq.

25
is obtained by
precomposing the evaluation map

\langle\Delta_{B},(C,c)\rangle,\Delta_{B}\rightarrow(C,c)
for

\Delta_{B}
described above, by the cartesian monad map
Eq.

30
.
∎

Running Example 3.3.9
.

In
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
, the hom

\llbracket\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\rrbracket=(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)
between monads

\mathcal{B}=(B,b)
and
\mathcal{C}=(C,c)
is the
\mathcal{V}
-category given
as follows. Its
object-set is
\underline{\smash{\mathsf{Mnd}}}(\mathbb{C})\bigl((B,b),(C,c)\bigr)
, which
by
3.3.6
is the set of
\mathcal{V}
-functors

\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
. As for its hom-objects, we have by
cartesianness of (
29
) and the
description of
\langle\Delta_{B},(C,c)\rangle
from
2.5.8

that

\llbracket\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\rrbracket(F,G)=\mathcal{C}^{B}\bigl((Fx)_{x\in B},(Gx)_{x\in B}\bigr)=\textstyle\prod_{x\in B}\mathcal{C}(Fx,Gx)\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

In particular, when
\mathcal{V}=\mathsf{Set}
, this
\llbracket\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\rrbracket
is the category of
functors
\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
and “unnatural
transformations”
\alpha\colon F\Rightarrow_{u}G
, i.e., families
of morphisms
\alpha_{x}\colon Fx\rightarrow Gx
satisfying no
further conditions.

From this result,
3.2.2
and
3.3.2
, we immediately obtain, under our running hypotheses:

Corollary 3.3.10
.

The closed symmetric multicategory
\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
of monads and monad multimorphisms is representable.

Finally, the next theorem accomplishes this section’s goal, namely that
the non-commuting tensor product of monads determines a
a symmetric monoidal closed structure on the category
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
.
We state explicitly all our assumptions for reference.

Theorem 3.3.11
.

Let
(\mathbb{C},\boxtimes,I)
be a
symmetric normal oplax monoidal closed double category. Under

I
,
III
,
IV
and
II
,
the category
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
of monads and monad morphisms in
\mathbb{C}
admits
the structure of a symmetric monoidal closed category, with tensor
product
\mathbin{\Box}
given by the non-commuting tensor product of monads,
and unit object given by the discrete monad
\Delta_{I}
on the unit
object of
\mathbb{C}
.

Proof.

The existence of the symmetric monoidal structure follows from
3.3.10
via
the symmetric version of
[
Her00
, Def. 9.6]
; the closedness then follows from
[
Man12
, Prop. 4.3]
.
∎

Remark 3.3.12
.

As already mentioned, there is a more direct way of constructing the non-commuting monoidal structure, which we have avoided since it will be less useful for the work to come. However, it may be helpful to see how it goes. We start from the definition of
\mathbin{\Box}
as in (
18
), and then construct associativity and unitality isomorphisms by hand, using an assumption mentioned above: that each functor
\Delta_{A}\boxtimes({\mathord{\text{--}}})\colon\mathsf{Mnd}_{B}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{Mnd}_{A\boxtimes B}(\mathbb{C})
preserves coproducts of monads. This will certainly be the case if
\mathbb{C}
is closed by virtue of
2.5.7
(ii).
In this situation the associativity constraint

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A\boxtimes B)\boxtimes C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A\boxtimes B)\boxtimes C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes(B\boxtimes C)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes(B\boxtimes C)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(a\mathbin{\Box}b)\mathbin{\Box}c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a\mathbin{\Box}(b\mathbin{\Box}c)}

has as vertical maps the associativity structure isomorphisms of
(\mathbb{C}_{0},\boxtimes)
, and
2
-morphism data given by the composite of invertible
2
-morphisms

\displaystyle(a\mathbin{\Box}b)\mathbin{\Box}c

\displaystyle=(a\mathbin{\Box}b)\boxtimes\Delta_{C}+\Delta_{A\boxtimes B}\boxtimes c=\left(a\boxtimes\Delta_{B}+\Delta_{A}\boxtimes b\right)\boxtimes\Delta_{C}+\Delta_{A\boxtimes B}\boxtimes c

\displaystyle\cong a\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\boxtimes\Delta_{C}+(\Delta_{A}\boxtimes b)\boxtimes\Delta_{C}+(\Delta_{A}\boxtimes\Delta_{B})\boxtimes c

\displaystyle\cong a\boxtimes\Delta_{B}\boxtimes\Delta_{C}+\Delta_{A}\boxtimes(b\boxtimes\Delta_{C})+\Delta_{A}\boxtimes(\Delta_{B}\boxtimes c)

\displaystyle\cong a\boxtimes\Delta_{B\boxtimes C}+\Delta_{A}\boxtimes(b\boxtimes\Delta_{C}+\Delta_{B}\boxtimes c)

\displaystyle=a\mathbin{\Box}(b\mathbin{\Box}c)\mathrlap{,}

where
3.3.3
and normality of
\mathbb{C}
are used. The construction of the unit isomorphisms is similar.

4.
The commuting tensor product of monads

Our objective in this section is to refine the non-commuting tensor
product of monads in
\mathbb{C}
of the preceding section to a

commuting tensor product
. Once again, this tensor product will
underlie a symmetric monoidal closed structure on
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
, and once
again, we will construct it by exhibiting a symmetric closed
multicategory, now of monads and
commuting monad
multimorphisms
.

4.1.
The multicategory of monads and commuting multimorphisms

As the nomenclature suggests, commutativity will be a property of a monad
multimorphism (
3.1.2
), which is most easily described in the binary case; we
thus begin with this. Much as in
[
GL16
]
, a key role
will be played by the
following maps derived from the oplax monoidal structure of
(\mathbb{C},\boxtimes)
:

Definition 4.1.1
.

Given horizontal cells
a_{1}\colon A_{1}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow A_{1}^{\prime}
and

a_{2}\colon A_{2}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow A_{2}
in
\mathbb{C}
, we define the globular

2
-morphisms
\sigma_{a_{1},a_{2}}
and
\tau_{a_{1},a_{2}}
as to the
left and right in:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}_{1}\boxtimes A^{\prime}_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}_{1}\boxtimes A^{\prime}_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}_{1}\boxtimes A^{\prime}_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(a_{1}\circ\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}})\boxtimes(\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}}\circ a_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\xi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2})}

and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}_{1}\boxtimes A^{\prime}_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}_{1}\boxtimes A^{\prime}_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}_{1}\boxtimes A^{\prime}_{2}\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\circ a_{1})\boxtimes(a_{2}\circ\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\xi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2})\circ(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}})}

Definition 4.1.2
.

We say
that a binary monad multimorphism

(f,\phi_{1},\phi_{2})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),(A_{2},a_{2})\rightarrow(B,b)
is
commuting
if the following diagram commutes in

\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
:

(31)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(B,b\circ b)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(B,b)\mathrlap{.}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},(\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2})\circ(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(B,b\circ b)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f,\phi_{1}\circ\phi_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\sigma)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\tau)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f,\phi_{2}\circ\phi_{1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}

Running Example 4.1.3
.

For
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
, under our standing assumption that
\mathcal{V}
is symmetric
monoidal closed with colimits, we have that:

\displaystyle(a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2})[(y_{1},y_{2});(x_{1},x_{2})]

\displaystyle=a_{1}[y_{1};x_{1}]\otimes a_{2}[y_{2};x_{2}]

\displaystyle((a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2}))[(y_{1},y_{2});(x_{1},x_{2})]

\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{(z_{1},z_{2})}a_{1}[y_{1};z_{1}]\otimes\delta_{y_{2}z_{2}}\otimes\delta_{z_{1}x_{1}}\otimes a_{2}[z_{2};x_{2}]

\displaystyle((\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2})\circ(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}}))[(y_{1},y_{2});(x_{1},x_{2})]

\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{(z_{1},z_{2})}\delta_{y_{1}z_{1}}\otimes a_{2}[y_{2};z_{2}]\otimes a_{2}[z_{1};x_{1}]\otimes\delta_{z_{2}x_{2}}\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

On summing over the
\delta
’s, the second and third of these
are isomorphic to
a_{1}[y_{1};x_{1}]\otimes a_{2}[y_{2};x_{2}]
and

a_{2}[y_{2};x_{2}]\otimes a_{1}[y_{1};x_{1}]
respectively, and modulo these
isomorphisms, the maps
\sigma
and
\tau
are just the identity and
the symmetry
\beta
of
\mathcal{V}
, respectively. Thus, we see that a

\mathcal{V}
-functor of two variables

F\colon\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{2}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
is commuting
precisely when each diagram of the form

(32)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}_{1}}(y_{1},x_{1})\otimes{\mathcal{A}_{2}}(y_{2},x_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}}(F(y_{1},y_{2}),F(x_{1},y_{2}))\otimes{\mathcal{B}}(F(x_{1},y_{2}),F(x_{1},x_{2}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}_{1}}(y_{1},x_{1})\otimes{\mathcal{A}_{2}}(y_{2},x_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}}(F(y_{1},y_{2}))\otimes{\mathcal{B}}(F(x_{1},x_{2}))\mathrlap{.}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}_{2}}(y_{2},x_{2})\otimes{\mathcal{A}_{1}}(y_{1},x_{1})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}}(F(y_{1},y_{2}),F(y_{1},x_{2}))\otimes{\mathcal{B}}(F(y_{1},x_{2}),F(x_{1},x_{2}))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F({\mathord{\text{--}}},y_{2})\otimes F(x_{1},{\mathord{\text{--}}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mu}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(y_{1},{\mathord{\text{--}}})\otimes F({\mathord{\text{--}}},x_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mu}

commutes in
\mathcal{V}
. As shown in
[
KML71
, §III.4]
, this is precisely what is required for

F
to extend to a bifunctor

\mathcal{A}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{A}_{2}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
, where
\otimes

is the usual tensor product of
\mathcal{V}
-categories over a symmetric
monoidal base
\mathcal{V}
.

Note that in this case, the notion of commutativity reconstructs
something with a simpler and more direct definition. The reason for
this, as noted in
2.5.3
, is that, when
\mathcal{V}
is
symmetric monoidal,
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
provides a slightly degenerate instance
of our framework. To lift this degeneracy, we may consider a base

\mathcal{V}
which is not symmetric monoidal, but only normal duoidal
with respect to tensor products
\circ
and
\boxtimes
. Then
\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})

is the multicategory of
(\mathcal{V},\circ)
-categories and

(\mathcal{V},\circ)
-functors of several variables—but the notion of
commutativity involves also the other tensor product
\boxtimes
. Indeed,
the maps
\sigma
and
\tau
will then (to within
codomain-isomorphism) have components of the form

a_{1}[y_{1};x_{1}]\boxtimes a_{2}[y_{2};x_{2}]\xrightarrow{\sigma}a_{1}[y_{1};x_{1}]\circ a_{2}[y_{2};x_{2}]\quad\text{and}\quad a_{1}[y_{1};x_{1}]\boxtimes a_{2}[y_{2};x_{2}]\xrightarrow{\tau}a_{2}[y_{2};x_{2}]\circ a_{1}[y_{1};x_{1}]\hbox to0.0pt{ ;\hss}

and the appropriate analogue of (
32
) will feature

{\mathcal{A}_{1}}(y_{1},x_{1})\boxtimes{\mathcal{A}_{2}}(y_{2},x_{2})
farthest to the
left, and with each other
\otimes
replaced by
\circ
. In this
way, we re-find precisely Definition 10 of
[
GL16
]
,
expressing the notion of
\mathcal{V}
-bifunctor over a normal duoidal
base
\mathcal{V}
.

We wish to extend this definition to arbitrary monad multimorphisms.
The idea is that a multimorphism

(f,\vec{\phi})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n})\to(B,b)
should
commute just when it commutes in each pair
(i,j)
of distinct input
arguments. There are two ways to go about setting this up formally.
One involves defining “
n
-ary interchanger”
2
-morphisms

(33)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes\dots\boxtimes A_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes C_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes A_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes B_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes C_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(y_{1}\circ x_{1})\boxtimes\,\cdots\,\boxtimes(y_{n}\circ x_{n})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\xi^{(n)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{1}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes x_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{1}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes y_{n}}

built recursively from the binary interchangers
\xi
, using these to
define
n
-ary analogues of the maps
\sigma
and
\tau

of
4.1.1
, and then setting up a hexagon, similar
to
Eq.

31
but more elaborate, which
expresses directly the
(i,j)
-commutativity of
(f,\vec{\phi})
.
However, we prefer to avoid this, and adopt the following “quick and
dirty” definition, which uses
3.1.1
:

Definition 4.1.4
.

Let

(f,\vec{\phi})=(f,\phi_{1},\dots,\phi_{n})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n})\to(B,b)
be a monad multimorphism and

1\leqslant i<j\leqslant n
. We say that
(f,\vec{\phi})

is
(i,j)
-commuting
if the binary multimorphism

(f,\phi_{i},\phi_{j})\colon\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[1,i\textrm{-}1]}\boxtimes(A_{i},a_{i})\boxtimes\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[i+1,j\textrm{-}1]},\,\,(A_{j},a_{j})\boxtimes\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[j+1,n]}\rightarrow(B,b)

is commuting. Where there is no scope for confusion, we may also say
that
(f,\vec{\phi})
is
(A_{i},A_{j})
-commuting
. We say that

(f,\smash{\vec{\phi}})
is
commuting
, we mean that it is

(i,j)
-commuting for all
1\leqslant i<j\leqslant n
.

The reason we term this definition “quick and dirty”, rather than
merely quick, is that we have chosen, in a slightly non-canonical way,
to attach the tensor of discrete monads

\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[i+1,j\textrm{-}1]}
to the first input argument of

(f,\phi_{i},\phi_{j})
; we could equally have attached it to the second
input argument, or indeed, have split it into two parts, one attached
to the first and one to the second. It is not hard to show that these
choices are irrelevant, for example by showing that each of them
yields the same notion of commutativity as the approach involving the

n
-ary interchangers (
33
).

The following lemma ensures that the symmetric multicategory structure of monads and monad multimorphisms (
3.1.4
) restricts to commuting monad multimorphisms in an appropriate way.

Lemma 4.1.5
.

Let
(f,\vec{\phi})\colon(B_{1},b_{1}),\dots,(B_{n},b_{n})\to(C,c)
and
(g,\vec{\psi})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{m},a_{m})\to(B_{k},b_{k})
be monad multimorphisms.

(1)

If
(f,\vec{\phi})
is
(i,j)
-commuting, and
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
, then
(f,\vec{\phi})\circ\sigma
is

(\sigma(i),\sigma(j))
-commuting.

(2)

If
(f,\vec{\phi})
is
(B_{i},B_{j})
-commuting for
i,j\neq k
, then

(f,\vec{\phi})\circ_{k}(g,\vec{\psi})
is
(B_{i},B_{j})
-commuting.

(3)

If
(f,\vec{\phi})
is
(B_{i},B_{k})
-commuting, then

(f,\vec{\phi})\circ_{k}(g,\vec{\psi})
is
(B_{i},A_{j})
-commuting for
all
1\leqslant j\leqslant m
.

(4)

If
(g,\vec{\psi})
is
(A_{i},A_{j})
-commuting,
then
(f,\vec{\phi})\circ_{k}(g,\vec{\psi})
is

(A_{i},A_{j})
-commuting.

Proof.

This is a straightforward diagram chase using the definitions of
commutativity and composition of monad multimorphisms, and the
irrelevance of the positioning of the medial elements

\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[i+1,j\textrm{-}1]}
.
∎

It immediately follows that:

Proposition 4.1.6
.

The monads and commuting monad multimorphisms form a sub-symmetric
multicategory
\mathsf{CMultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
of

\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
.

4.2.
Pre-representability of
\mathsf{CMultMnd}(\mathbb{C})

Our goal now is to show that the symmetric multicategory of commuting
multimorphisms in
\mathbb{C}
is representable. We have already seen one
case where already know this is true; indeed, when
\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
for
a symmetric monoidal closed cocomplete
\mathcal{V}
, we argued
in
4.1.3
that the universal binary commuting
multimorphism should be represented by the usual tensor product of

\mathcal{V}
-categories. However, in general it is the case that further
work will be required.

As in
Section

3.2
, we begin this work by constructing
pre-universal nullary and binary commuting multimorphisms. For this,
we assume that
\mathbb{C}
satisfies

I
,
II
,
III
and
IV

of
Section

3
, as well as the following two further
hypotheses:

Assumption V
.

Each forgetful functor

\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
has a left adjoint

\textsf{Free}\colon\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
.

Assumption VI
.

Each category
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C})
has
coequalisers.

Note that, since we have already assumed
\mathbb{C}
to be
fibrant,
V
together
with
2.2.6
tells us that
\mathbb{C}
admits free
monads in the sense of
2.2.4
, i.e., that the forgetful
functor
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
has a left adjoint over
\mathbb{C}_{0}
, denoted by
\textsf{Free}(-)
.
Similarly, fibrancy,
VI
and

2.4.4
(ii) together tell us that
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
admits all
coequalisers of identity-on-objects parallel pairs.

The following is the counterpart of
3.2.2
, establishing the existence of nullary and binary pre-universal multimorphisms.

Proposition 4.2.1
.

The multicategory
\mathsf{CMultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
is pre-representable.

Proof.

Since nullary multimorphisms always commute, the universal nullary
multimorphism
\ \rightarrow\Delta_{I}
is also a universal nullary
commuting multimorphisms. For the binary case, we must show that,
for all
(A_{1},a_{1}),(A_{2},a_{2})\in\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
, there is a pre-universal
binary commuting multimorphism

(34)

(1_{A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}},\eta_{1},\eta_{2})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),(A_{2},a_{2})\rightarrow(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\otimes a_{2})\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

In order to construct this, we start from the universal (non-commuting) binary
multimorphism

(1_{A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}},\iota_{1},\iota_{2})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),(A_{2},a_{2})\rightarrow(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\mathbin{\Box}a_{2})

of
Eq.

20
, and consider the
hexagon
Eq.

35
in
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
which
would express its
(1,2)
-commutativity:

(35)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},(a_{1}\mathbin{\Box}a_{2})\circ(a_{1}\mathbin{\Box}a_{2}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\mathbin{\Box}a_{2})\mathrlap{.}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},(\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2})\circ(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},(a_{1}\mathbin{\Box}a_{2})\circ(a_{1}\mathbin{\Box}a_{2}))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\iota_{1}\circ\iota_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\sigma)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\tau)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\iota_{2}\circ\iota_{1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}

There is, of course, no reason to believe that this hexagon will
commute in general, but we can quotient
a_{1}\mathbin{\Box}a_{2}
to bring this about.
Since
a_{1}\mathbin{\Box}a_{2}
bears a monad structure, we may transpose the
two sides of the hexagon above to obtain a parallel pair of maps in

\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
, as to the left in:

(36)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},\textsf{Free}(a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\mathbin{\Box}a_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\otimes a_{2})\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathrm{id},\upsilon_{1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathrm{id},\upsilon_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathrm{id},q)}

Now by the remarks above, this identity-on-objects pair admits a
coequaliser in
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
as to the right. We claim that the object

(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\otimes a_{2})
so obtained is pre-universal, when
equipped with the multimorphism
Eq.

34

given by the composite

(\mathrm{id},q)\circ(1_{A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}},\iota_{1},\iota_{2})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),(A_{2},a_{2})\rightarrow(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\otimes a_{2})\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

To establish the claim, let

(f,\phi_{1},\phi_{2})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),(A_{2},a_{2})\rightarrow(B,b)

be a commuting monad multimorphism. Since
(f,\phi_{1},\phi_{2})
is
in particular a monad multimorphism, it factors uniquely through the
universal binary
multimorphism
Eq.

20
, as

(f,\bar{\phi})\colon(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\mathbin{\Box}a_{2})\rightarrow(B,b)
say. It thus suffices to show that this
(f,\bar{\phi})

factors (necessarily uniquely) through the coequaliser

(\mathrm{id},q)\colon a\mathbin{\Box}b\twoheadrightarrow a\otimes b
. In
other words, we must show that composing with
(f,\bar{\phi})

makes equal the maps
(\mathrm{id},\upsilon_{1})
and
(\mathrm{id},\upsilon_{2})

in
Eq.

36
.
Transposing under the free-forgetful adjunction, this is equally to
ask that the hexagon
Eq.

35

commutes upon postcomposition by
(f,\bar{\phi})
. But since

(f,\bar{\phi})
is a monad morphism and since

(f,\bar{\phi})\circ(\mathrm{id},\iota_{1},\iota_{2})=(f,\phi_{1},\phi_{2})
, this postcomposition is precisely the hexagon expressing
the
(1,2)
-commutativity of
(f,\phi_{1},\phi_{2})
.
∎

Like before, there is no obstacle to extending the above result to
exhibit universal
n
-ary commuting multimorphisms: we start from the
universal non-commuting
n
-ary multimorphism, and then take repeated
coequalisers to impose
(i,j)
-commutativity for all
i<j
. But,
like before, we do not need to give this argument in full, since it
will follow once we have established
closedness
of our
multicategory.

4.3.
Closure and representability of
\mathsf{CMultMnd}(\mathbb{C})

In this section, we
build the internal homs which exhibit

\mathsf{CMultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
as a closed multicategory. We do so using the
corresponding internal homs of
\mathsf{MultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
(see

3.3.8
), and as a first step we record how
these interact with commutativity.

Lemma 4.3.1
.

A monad multimorphism

(f,\phi_{1},\dots,\phi_{n},\psi)\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n}),(B,b)\rightarrow(C,c)
is
(A_{i},A_{j})
-commuting if and
only if its transpose

(\bar{f},\bar{\phi}_{1},\dots,\bar{\phi}_{n})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n})\rightarrow\llbracket(B,b),(C,c)\rrbracket
is

(A_{i},A_{j})
-commuting.

Proof.

Note that by
4.1.4
,
(f,\vec{\phi},\psi)
is
(A_{i},A_{j})
-commuting if and
only if

(37)

(f,\phi_{i},\phi_{j},\psi)\colon\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[1,i\textrm{-}1]}\boxtimes(A_{i},a_{i})\boxtimes\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[i+1,j\textrm{-}1]},\,\,(A_{j},a_{j})\boxtimes\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[j+1,n]}\boxtimes(B,b)\rightarrow(C,c)

is
(A_{i},A_{j})
-commuting, while its transpose is
(A_{i},A_{j})
-commuting if and only if

(38)

(f,\bar{\phi}_{i},\bar{\phi}_{j})\colon\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[1,i\textrm{-}1]}\boxtimes(A_{i},a_{i})\boxtimes\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[i+1,j\textrm{-}1]},\,\,(A_{j},a_{j})\boxtimes\mathchoice{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\displaystyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\textstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptstyle)$}}}}}{\mathopen{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle($}}}}\Delta_{A}\mathclose{\smash{\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{\scalebox{0.7}[1]{$\scriptscriptstyle)$}}}}}_{[j+1,n]}\rightarrow\llbracket(B,b),(C,c)\rrbracket

is
(A_{i},A_{j})
-commuting. It is easy to see
that
Eq.

37
and

Eq.

38
are themselves paired under
transpose, so that without loss of generality we may reduce to the
case
n=2
.

On doing so, to say that

(\bar{f},\bar{\phi}_{1},\bar{\phi}_{2})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),(A_{2},a_{2})\rightarrow\llbracket(B,b),(C,c)\rrbracket
is
(A_{1},A_{2})
-commuting is to
say that the following hexagon commutes:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket\circ\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},(\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2})\circ(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket\circ\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\bar{f},{\bar{\phi}}_{1}\circ{\bar{\phi}}_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\sigma)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\tau)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\bar{f},{\bar{\phi}}_{2}\circ{\bar{\phi}}_{1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}

where the underlying object
\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0}
in
\mathbb{C}_{0}
is the the object
\underline{\smash{\mathsf{Mnd}}}(\mathbb{C})(b,c)\in\mathbb{C}_{0}
of
3.3.5
like before. Clearly, we have commutativity at the level of underlying maps in

\mathbb{C}_{0}
; so it suffices to show commutativity after postcomposition
by the map
Eq.

29
, which is cartesian with respect to both forgetful functors
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
and
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
. This postcomposition is equally well the
hexagon:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\langle B,C\rangle,\langle\mathrm{id}_{B},c\rangle\circ\langle\mathrm{id}_{B},c\rangle)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\langle B,C\rangle,\langle\mathrm{id}_{B},c\rangle)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},(\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2})\circ(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\langle B,C\rangle,\langle\mathrm{id}_{B},c\rangle\circ\langle\mathrm{id}_{B},c\rangle)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\tilde{f},{\tilde{\phi}}_{1}\circ{\tilde{\phi}}_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\sigma)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\tau)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\tilde{f},{\tilde{\phi}}_{2}\circ{\tilde{\phi}}_{1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}

where
\tilde{f}
,
\tilde{\phi}_{1}
,
\tilde{\phi}_{2}
are transposes of

f
,
\phi_{1}
,
\phi_{2}
under the adjunctions

({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes B\dashv\langle B,{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle
and

({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B}\dashv\langle\mathrm{id}_{B},{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle
.

Now, by the
definition of the multiplication
\mu
of the monad
\bigl(\langle B,C\rangle,\langle\mathrm{id}_{B},c\rangle\bigr)
in
Eq.

14
together with
the naturality of
\zeta
therein, the transpose of the composite

(1,\mu)(\tilde{f},\tilde{\phi}_{1}\circ\tilde{\phi}_{2})
under

({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes(B,\mathrm{id}_{B})\dashv\langle(B,\mathrm{id}_{B}),{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle
is the composite

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}\boxtimes B,((a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2}))\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(C,c)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}\boxtimes B,(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{A_{2}}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(C,c\circ c)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\zeta)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f,\phi_{1}\circ\phi_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}

and correspondingly for
(1,\mu)(\tilde{f},\tilde{\phi}_{2}\circ\tilde{\phi}_{1})
. Thus, the hexagon above commutes just when the the outside
of the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(A_{1}\!\boxtimes A_{2}\!\boxtimes\!B,((a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id})\!\circ\!(\mathrm{id}\boxtimes a_{2}))\boxtimes\mathrm{id})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\!\boxtimes A_{2}\!\boxtimes\!B,(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}\boxtimes\mathrm{id})\!\circ\!(\mathrm{id}\boxtimes a_{2}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(C,c\!\circ\!c)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\!\boxtimes A_{2}\!\boxtimes\!B,(a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2})\boxtimes\mathrm{id})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(A_{1}\!\boxtimes A_{2}\!\boxtimes\!B,(a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2})\boxtimes\mathrm{id})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(C,c)\mathrlap{.}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\!\boxtimes A_{2}\!\boxtimes\!B,((\mathrm{id}\boxtimes a_{2})\!\circ\!(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}))\boxtimes\mathrm{id})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\!\boxtimes A_{2}\!\boxtimes\!B,(a_{1}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}\boxtimes\mathrm{id})\!\circ\!(\mathrm{id}\boxtimes a_{2}\boxtimes\mathrm{id}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(C,c\!\circ\!c)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\zeta)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f,{\phi}_{1}\circ{\phi}_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\sigma\boxtimes 1)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\tau\boxtimes 1)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\sigma)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\tau)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\zeta)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f,{\phi}_{2}\circ{\phi}_{1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}

commutes. Since the left two regions of this diagram commute by the
normal oplax monoidal coherence axioms, and since the associativity
constraint centre left is invertible, we conclude that the outside
commutes just when the right hexagon commutes. But this hexagon
expresses precisely the
(A_{1},A_{2})
-commutativity of

(f,\phi_{1},\phi_{2},\psi)
. Thus, we have shown that

(\bar{f},\bar{\phi}_{1},\bar{\phi}_{2})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),(A_{2},a_{2})\rightarrow\llbracket(B,b),(C,c)\rrbracket
is
(A_{1},A_{2})
-commuting just
when
(f,\phi_{1},\phi_{2},\psi)\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),(A_{2},a_{2}),(B,b)\rightarrow(C,c)
is so, as required.
∎

We will require one further result before exhibiting the closed
structure of
\mathsf{CMultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
; informally speaking, this establishes
that, for a binary multimorphism

(A_{1},a_{1}),(A_{2},a_{2})\rightarrow(B,b)
, the (generalised) elements
of
(A_{1},a_{1})
which commute with
(A_{2},a_{2})
are closed under
composition.

Lemma 4.3.2
.

Let
(f,\phi_{1},\phi_{2})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),(A_{2},a_{2})\rightarrow(B,b)
be a monad multimorphism, and consider the
hexagon (
31
) which would express
the commutativity of
f
.

(1)

This hexagon always
commutes on precomposition by the map

(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2})\xrightarrow{(1,\eta\boxtimes 1)}(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2})\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

(2)

If this hexagon
commutes on precomposition by maps

(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}^{\prime}\boxtimes a_{2})\xrightarrow{(1,u\boxtimes 1)}(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2})\quad\text{and}\quad(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}^{\prime\prime}\boxtimes a_{2})\xrightarrow{(1,v\boxtimes 1)}(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2})

then it also commutes on precomposition by the map

(39)

(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},(a_{1}^{\prime}\circ a_{1}^{\prime\prime})\boxtimes a_{2})\xrightarrow{(1,(u\circ v)\boxtimes 1)}(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},(a_{1}\circ a_{1})\boxtimes a_{2})\xrightarrow{(1,\mu\boxtimes 1)}(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2})\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

Proof.

Both parts are proved in an identical fashion, so we concentrate on
the more involved case of (ii).
For this, note that the top path
around (
31
) becomes the composite
below left on precomposition by (
39
), which by
naturality of
\sigma
, is equally the composite to the right:

Here, we have additionally used the naturality of
\xi
and the unit
constraints of
\mathbb{C}
to commute
u\boxtimes 1
and
v\boxtimes 1
past
them. Now, since
\sigma
is built using the interchanger
\xi
and
coherences for
\mathbb{C}
, a straightforward coherence calculation shows
that the first three rows to the left above are equally well the
first three rows to the right; therein, we have also used
associativity for the monad
(B,b)
to rewrite the bottom two rows.

Considering the pasting so obtained, note that by naturality of

\sigma
, we may move
v\boxtimes 1
above
\sigma
, and on doing so,
the resulting diagram contains a copy of the top path
of (
31
), precomposed by

v\boxtimes 1
. By our assumption, this is equal to the bottom path
of (
31
) precomposed by

v\boxtimes 1
; so rewriting by this, and using naturality of
\sigma

again, we see that the pasting above right is equally the pasting to
the left in:
