Finally, using oplax monoidal coherence, we can rewrite the top
three rows as the top two rows to the right above; we also rewrite
the bottom two rows using the evident notation

\mu^{(3)}=\mu(\mu\circ 1)=\mu(1\circ\mu)
. Note that the
resulting diagram is perfectly symmetrical; whence, by a
symmetric argument, we may also reduce the lower side
of (
31
), precomposed
by (
39
), to the same composite. This
establishes (ii).

We leave the simpler case of (i) to the reader, who by following the
same kind of argument as above, should have no difficulty in verifying that, on precomposition by
(1,\eta\boxtimes 1)
,
both paths around (
31
) are equal
to

(f,\phi_{2})\colon(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},\mathrm{id}_{A_{1}}\boxtimes a_{2})\rightarrow(B,b)
.
∎

We now proceed to exhibit the closed structure of
\mathsf{CMultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
. For
this, we will need, in addition to our previous assumptions:

Assumption VII
.

\mathbb{C}
has local equalisers.

Since
\mathbb{C}_{0}
has equalisers by
III
, it follows
from this assumption and
2.4.2
that
\mathbb{C}
has
parallel equalisers. Thus, by
2.4.3
(i), so does
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
.

Proposition 4.3.3
.

The symmetric multicategory
\mathsf{CMultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
is closed. That is, for all

(B,b),(C,c)\in\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
, there exists a hom-object
[(B,b),(C,c)]
and binary multimorphism

(e^{c},\varepsilon^{c}_{1},\varepsilon^{c}_{2})\colon[(B,b),(C,c)],(B,b)\rightarrow(C,c)

composition with which establishes a bijection of multimorphism-sets

(40)

\begin{array}[]{r@{\,}l@{\ }c@{\ }ll}(f,\phi_{1},\dots,\phi_{n},\psi)\colon&(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n}),(B,b)&\longrightarrow&(C,c)&\text{ commuting}\\
\vskip 3.0pt\cr\hline\cr\vskip 3.0pt\cr(\bar{f},\bar{\phi}_{1},\dots,\bar{\phi}_{n})\colon&(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n})&\longrightarrow&[(B,b),(C,c)]&\text{ commuting}\end{array}

Proof.

Consider the binary multimorphism

(e,\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2})\colon\llbracket(B,b),(C,c)\rrbracket,(B,b)\rightarrow(C,c)
providing, as
in
Eq.

25
, the evaluation map of the
non-commuting internal hom. The following is the hexagon which would
express that this is a commuting binary multimorphism:

(41)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0}\boxtimes B,(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0}}\boxtimes b))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(C,c\circ c)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0}\boxtimes B,\llbracket b,c\rrbracket\boxtimes b)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(C,c)\mathrlap{.}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0}\boxtimes B,(\mathrm{id}_{\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0}}\boxtimes b)\circ(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(C,c\circ c)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(e,\varepsilon_{1}\circ\varepsilon_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\sigma)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\tau)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(e,\varepsilon_{2}\circ\varepsilon_{1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}

Like before, there is no reason to expect this diagram to commute in general.
However, the composites around the top and bottom sides constitute a
parallel pair of maps
(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)\boxtimes(B,b)\rightarrow(C,c)
, and taking their transposes with respect to
the closed structure of
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
, we obtain a parallel pair as to the
right in:

(42)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces([b,c]_{0},[b,c])}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle(B,b),(C,c)\rangle\hbox to0.0pt{ ,\hss}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\kappa)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(i,\nu_{1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(i,\nu_{2})}}

where
i\colon\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0}\rightarrow\langle B,C\rangle
is as
in
Eq.

29
.
By
VII
and the remarks following,
this pair admits an equaliser in
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
as displayed. We will show
that the subobject of
(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)
so obtained is
in fact a submonad, and that it represents the desired internal hom
in
\mathsf{CMultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
.

Towards the first of these goals, observe that a map

(f,\phi)\colon(A,x)\rightarrow(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)

in
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
factors through
(1,\kappa)
precisely when

({\mathord{\text{--}}})\circ(f,\phi)
renders the two maps
(i,\nu_{1})
and

(i,\nu_{2})
equal; which, by transposing under the adjunction

({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes(B,b)\dashv\langle(B,b),{\mathord{\text{--}}}\rangle
on
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
, happens
just when the hexagon (
41
) commutes on
precomposition by
(f\boxtimes 1_{B},\phi\boxtimes 1_{B})
. In particular,
(
41
) will commute on precomposition by

(1,\kappa\boxtimes 1)
. Using these observations, we can now show that

([b,c]_{0},[b,c])
is a submonad of

(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)
. It is enough to show that
there are factorisations as to the left and right in:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces([b,c]_{0},\mathrm{id}_{[b,c]_{0}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces([b,c]_{0},[b,c])}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\mathrm{id}_{\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\kappa)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\eta)}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces([b,c]_{0},[b,c]\circ[b,c])}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces([b,c]_{0},[b,c])}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket\circ\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\kappa\circ\kappa)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\kappa)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}

where
\eta
and
\mu
are the maps exhibiting the monad structure
of
\llbracket b,c\rrbracket
. But to say that
(1,\eta)
factors through

(1,\kappa)
is equivalent to saying that (
41
)
commutes on precomposition by
(1,\eta\boxtimes 1)
, which is indeed the case
by
4.3.2
(i). On the other
hand, to say
that
(1,\mu)(1,\kappa\circ\kappa)
factors through

(1,\kappa)
is to say that (
41
)
commutes on precomposition by

([b,c]_{0}\boxtimes B,([b,c]\circ[b,c])\boxtimes B)\xrightarrow{(1,(\kappa\circ\kappa)\boxtimes 1)}(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0}\boxtimes B,(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket\circ\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)\boxtimes B)\xrightarrow{(1,\mu\boxtimes 1)}(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0}\boxtimes B,\llbracket b,c\rrbracket\boxtimes B)\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

But we observed above that (
41
) commutes
on precomposition by
(1,\kappa\boxtimes 1)
; whence this follows
by
4.3.2
(ii). Thus

([b,c]_{0},[b,c])
is a submonad of

(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)
; it remains to prove that it provides
an internal hom in
\mathsf{CMultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
.

To this end, we show the following: given

(f,\vec{\phi},\psi)\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n}),(B,b)\rightarrow(C,c)
a monad multimorphism, its transpose

(\bar{f},\bar{\phi}_{1},\dots,\bar{\phi}_{n})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n})\rightarrow(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)
factors
through the subobject

([b,c]_{0},[b,c])\rightarrowtail(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)
just when
(f,\vec{\phi},\psi)
is

(A_{i},B)
-commuting for all
i
. By arguing as at the start of the
proof of
4.3.1
, we may immediately
reduce to the case
n=1
. Thus, suppose that

(f,\phi,\psi)\colon(A,a),(B,b)\rightarrow(C,c)
. To say that

(\bar{f},\bar{\phi})\colon(A,a)\rightarrow(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)
factors through
([b,c]_{0},[b,c])
is
precisely to say that
Eq.

41
commutes on
precomposition by
(\bar{f},\bar{\phi})
. But by naturality of

\sigma
and
\tau
and definition of transpose, this is precisely
to say that the following hexagon commutes:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A\boxtimes B,(a\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{A}\boxtimes b))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(C,c\circ c)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A\boxtimes B,a\boxtimes b)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(C,c)\mathrlap{,}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A\boxtimes B,(\mathrm{id}_{A}\boxtimes b)\circ(a\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{B}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(C,c\circ c)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f,\phi_{1}\circ\phi_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\sigma)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\tau)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f,\phi_{2}\circ\phi_{1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(1,\mu)}

on in other words, that
(f,\phi,\psi)
is
(A,B)
-commuting.

We now establish that
([b,c]_{0},[b,c])
is the internal
hom of
(B,b)
and
(C,c)
in
\mathsf{CMultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
. Indeed, by
3.3.8
, we have bijections between
sets of (not necessarily commuting) monad multimorphisms of the form:

\begin{array}[]{r@{\,}l@{\ }c@{\ }l}(f,\phi_{1},\dots,\phi_{n},\psi)\colon&(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n}),(B,b)&\longrightarrow&(C,c)\\
\vskip 3.0pt\cr\hline\cr\vskip 3.0pt\cr(\bar{f},\bar{\phi}_{1},\dots,\bar{\phi}_{n})\colon&(A_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(A_{n},a_{n})&\longrightarrow&\llbracket(B,b),(C,c)\rrbracket\end{array}

By
4.3.1
, a multimorphism as to the
top is
(A_{i},A_{j})
-commuting for all
i<j
just when the
corresponding multimorphism as below is commuting. By the result
just established, a multimorphism as to the top is
(A_{i},B)
-commuting for all
i
just when the corresponding multimorphism
as below factors through
[(B,b),(C,c)]
. Thus, the above
bijection restricts to a
bijection (
40
) as desired.
∎

Running Example 4.3.4
.

We saw in
3.3.9
that, when
\mathcal{V}
is symmetric
monoidal closed with products, the non-commuting hom

(\llbracket b,c\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket b,c\rrbracket)
between monads
\mathcal{B}=(B,b)
and

\mathcal{C}=(C,c)
is the
\mathcal{V}
-category
\llbracket\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\rrbracket

with as objects, the
\mathcal{V}
-functors
\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
,
and with homs given by the
\mathcal{V}
-objects of “unnatural

\mathcal{V}
-transformations”, i.e.
\llbracket\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\rrbracket(F,G)=\textstyle\prod_{x\in B}\mathcal{C}(Fx,Gx)
.

We now describe the corresponding commuting hom

[\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}]
. This is defined from the non-commuting one
by the equaliser (
42
). The objects of
this equaliser are the same, namely, the
\mathcal{V}
-functors

\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
. As for the homs, these are given
componentwise by the equaliser

[\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}](F,G)\xrightarrow{}\textstyle\prod_{x\in B}\mathcal{C}(Fx,Gx)\rightrightarrows\prod_{y,y^{\prime}\in B}[\mathcal{B}(y,y^{\prime}),\mathcal{C}(Fy,Gy^{\prime})]

in
\mathcal{V}
, where the parallel maps seen here have respective
components at
(y,y^{\prime})\in B\times B
given by

\displaystyle\textstyle\prod_{x\in B}\mathcal{C}(Fx,Gx)\xrightarrow{\pi_{y}}\mathcal{C}(Fy,Gy)\xrightarrow{\ \bar{\circ}\ }[\mathcal{C}(Gy,Gy^{\prime}),\mathcal{C}(Fy,Gy^{\prime})]\xrightarrow{[G_{yy^{\prime}},1]}[\mathcal{B}(y,y^{\prime}),\mathcal{C}(Fy,Gy^{\prime})]

\displaystyle\textstyle\prod_{x\in B}\mathcal{C}(Fx,Gx)\xrightarrow{\pi_{y^{\prime}}}\mathcal{C}(Fy^{\prime},Gy^{\prime})\xrightarrow{\ \bar{\circ}\ }[\mathcal{C}(Fy^{\prime},Gy^{\prime}),\mathcal{C}(Fy,Fy^{\prime})]\xrightarrow{[1,F_{yy^{\prime}}]}[\mathcal{B}(y,y^{\prime}),\mathcal{C}(Fy,Gy^{\prime})]\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

This equaliser is precisely the
\mathcal{V}
-enriched end

\int_{x\in\mathcal{B}}\mathcal{C}(Fx,Gx)
giving the
\mathcal{V}
-object of

\mathcal{V}
-natural transformations from
F
to

G

[
Kel82
, §2.2]
, so that
[\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}]
is
the usual functor
\mathcal{V}
-category.

Copying the proof of
3.3.10
mutatis
mutandis we conclude that:

Proposition 4.3.5
.

The symmetric multicategory
\mathsf{CMultMnd}(\mathbb{C})
of monads and commuting monad
multimorphisms is representable.

Now arguing as before and in analogy to
3.3.11
, we obtain the main result of this section. See
Table

2
for the list of assumptions.

Theorem 4.3.6
.

Let
(\mathbb{C},\boxtimes,I)
be a symmetric normal oplax monoidal closed
double category. Under

I
,
II
,
III
,
IV
,
V
,
VI
,
III
and
VII
,
the category
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
of monads and monad morphisms admits the
structure of a symmetric monoidal closed category, with tensor
product
\otimes
given by the commuting tensor product of monads,
and unit object given by the discrete monad
\Delta_{I}
on the unit
object
I
of
\mathbb{C}
.

5.
The commuting tensor product of bimodules

Our aim in this section is to extend the commuting tensor
product of monads and monad morphisms constructed in
Section

4
to
monad bimodules (cf.
2.3.1
).
In our applications in
Section

6
, this will yield the notion of commuting
tensor product of profunctors (between categories) and of symmetric multiprofunctors
(between symmetric multicategories).

We continue to work with a symmetric normal oplax monoidal double
category
(\mathbb{C},\boxtimes,I)
whose monoidal structure is closed, and for
which
\mathbb{C}
satisfies

I
,
II
,
III
,
IV
,
V
,
VI
and
VII
.
As we have seen (
4.3.6
), these conditions are sufficient for there to be a
“commuting” monoidal structure on the category of monads and monad
morphisms in
\mathbb{C}
. In order to extend this to bimodules, we make the following additional
assumption.

Assumption VIII
.

The double category
\mathbb{C}
has stable local reflexive coequalisers, as in
2.4.1
.

Thanks to this, we can apply
2.3.4
in order to
assemble the monads, monad morphisms and monad bimodules in
\mathbb{C}

into a double category written
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
. As we are assuming
\mathbb{C}
is
fibrant (
I
), the double category
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
is fibrant
by
2.3.4
.

5.1.
The multicategory of bimodules and commuting bimodule multimorphisms

We now embark on constructing the “commuting” monoidal structure on

\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
. For the vertical category
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})_{0}
, this is a mere rephrasing of

4.3.6
.

Proposition 5.1.1
.

The vertical category of
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
admits a symmetric monoidal closed structure given on objects by the commuting tensor product of monads.

Proof.

The vertical category
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})_{0}
is
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{C})
, the category
of monads and monad morphisms in
\mathbb{C}
, so the claim
follows from
4.3.6
.
∎

In order to extend the commuting tensor product to the category

\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})_{1}
, i.e. the category of bimodules and bimodule morphisms, we
follow a similar pattern to that followed in

Sections

3
and
4
: we show that the category

\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})_{1}
is the underlying category of a representable symmetric multicategory and
therefore admits a symmetric monoidal structure. Besides giving us the symmetric
monoidal structure, this also allows us to characterise the commuting tensor product of bimodules
by a universal property. For this, we now introduce the notion of
commuting multimorphism of bimodules (cf.
4.1.4
).

Definition 5.1.2
.

Let
p_{1}\colon(A_{1},a_{1})\hbox to38pt{\vbox to5.6pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 18.99997pt\lower-0.5pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{}{}{}{}{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}}{{}}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{}{{
{}{}}}{
{}{}}
{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-22.0pt}{0.0pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}}}{{}}{{}}}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
{
{}{}{}}{}{
{}{}{}}

2
-morphisms labelled as
\xi
are built inductively from
the binary interchangers of
2.5.1
in the evident manner.

Proposition 5.1.3
.

There is a symmetric multicategory
\mathsf{CMultBim}(\mathbb{C})
with bimodules as objects and
commuting bimodule multimorphisms as maps.

Proof.

Consider conditions
1
,
2
and
3
for a
commuting bimodule multimorphism.

Items

1
and
2
compose as they do in

\mathsf{CMultMnd}
, while
Item

3
composes as
in (the underlying multicategory of) the monoidal category
\mathbb{C}_{1}
.
It is routine to verify the bimodule compatibility conditions of a
multimorphism are stable under this composition.
∎

Note that there is no obstruction to defining a corresponding
multicategory
\mathsf{MultBim}(\mathbb{C})
of
not-necessarily-commuting bimodule multimorphisms. However, our
primary interest is in the commuting case and—by contrast with the
situation of the preceding two sections—the argument for the case of
commuting bimodule multimorphisms can be given without developing the
non-commuting case first. As such, we leave further consideration of

\mathsf{MultBim}(\mathbb{C})
to the reader.

5.2.
Pre-representability of
\mathsf{CMultBim}(\mathbb{C})

Our aim is to show that the multicategory
\mathsf{CMultBim}(\mathbb{C})
of
bimodules and commuting bimodule multimorphisms in
\mathbb{C}
is
representable. Our strategy for doing so will diverge from that of the
previous sections, but will at least begin in the same way: by establishing
pre-representability.

We first prove a lemma that rephrases the conditions to be a binary
module multimorphism as in
5.1.2
. Recall
the universal commuting binary
multimorphism (
34
) associated to
monads
(A_{1},a_{1})
and
(A_{2},a_{2})
, which has the form

(1_{A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}},\eta_{1},\eta_{2})\colon(A_{1},a_{1}),(A_{2},a_{2})\rightarrow(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\otimes a_{2})\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

By construction, the two sides of the
hexagon (
31
) expressing
commutativity of this multimorphism are equal; let us write their
common composite in
\mathsf{End}(\mathbb{C})
as:

(43)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2})}

Proposition 5.2.2
.

The symmetric multicategory
\mathsf{CMultBim}(\mathbb{C})
of bimodules and commuting bimodule morphisms
is pre-representable.

Proof.

The nullary case is immediate: the representing object is the
identity bimodule
I
on the discrete monad
\nabla{I}
. For the
binary case, consider the upper parts of the two sides of the
equality (
44
):

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(b_{1}\circ p_{1}\circ a_{1})\boxtimes(b_{2}\circ p_{2}\circ a_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\alpha_{1}\boxtimes\alpha_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}\boxtimes p_{2}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(b_{1}\circ p_{1}\circ a_{1})\boxtimes(b_{2}\circ p_{2}\circ a_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\xi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\pi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}\boxtimes p_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b_{1}\boxtimes b_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\pi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{1}\otimes a_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}\boxtimes p_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b_{1}\otimes b_{2}}

These are, respectively, maps

\displaystyle u\colon F_{a_{1},b_{1}}(p_{1})\boxtimes F_{a_{2},b_{2}}(p_{2})

\displaystyle\rightarrow p_{1}\boxtimes p_{2}

\displaystyle\text{and}\ \ v\colon F_{a_{1},b_{1}}(p_{1})\boxtimes F_{a_{2},b_{2}}(p_{2})

\displaystyle\rightarrow F_{a_{1}\otimes a_{2},b_{1}\otimes b_{2}}(p_{1}\boxtimes p_{2})

in
\mathbb{C}[A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}]
, and so we obtain a parallel pair of bimodule maps as to
the left in:

(46)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{a_{1}\otimes a_{2},b_{1}\otimes b_{2}}\big(F_{a_{1},b_{1}}(p_{1})\boxtimes F_{a_{2},b_{2}}(p_{2})\big)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{a_{1}\otimes a_{2},b_{1}\otimes b_{2}}(p_{1}\boxtimes p_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}\otimes p_{2}\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bar{v}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{a_{1}\otimes a_{2},b_{1}\otimes b_{2}}(u)}

Here, the upper arrow is the free bimodule morphism on
u
, while

\bar{v}
is the unique extension of
v
to a bimodule morphism. It
is easy to see that this
parallel pair is reflexive, with common splitting given by
F_{a_{1}\otimes a_{2},b_{1}\otimes b_{2}}(\eta,\eta)
. Thus, since

\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})[(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\otimes a_{2}),(B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2},b_{1}\otimes b_{2})]
has reflexive coequalisers, we can form the coequaliser of
this pair, as to the right.

By
2.4.4
(i), this coequaliser is also a
coequaliser in
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})_{1}
. Using this and the enhanced freeness
property of free bimodules described
in
2.3.10
, we see that a map out of

p_{1}\otimes p_{2}
in
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})_{1}
into an object

q\colon(C,c)\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow(D,d)
is equally well given by:

(1)

a map
(A_{1},a_{1})\otimes(A_{2},a_{2})\rightarrow(C,c)
;

(2)

a map
(B_{1},b_{1})\otimes(B_{2},b_{2})\rightarrow(D,d)
; and

(3)

a
2
-morphism

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes\ldots\boxtimes A_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes\ldots\boxtimes B_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D\hbox to0.0pt{ ,\hss}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}\boxtimes\ldots\boxtimes p_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\theta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}

such that the induced map

F_{a_{1}\otimes a_{2},b_{1}\otimes b_{2}}(p_{1}\boxtimes p_{2})\xrightarrow{\bar{\theta}}q
equalises the parallel pair
in (
46
). Clearly, the data
(i)–(iii) above can be equated with the data (i)–(iii)
of
5.1.2
; and a short argument with
adjointness shows that the equalising property is equivalent to the
equality (
44
), which,
by
5.2.1
is equally to say that these
data describe a commuting bimodule bimorphism.
∎

5.3.
Representability of
\mathsf{CMultBim}(\mathbb{C})

At this point, our development proceeds in a different direction to
previously. Rather than establish closedness of the multicategory

\mathsf{CMultBim}(\mathbb{C})
, and conclude
using
3.3.2
, we will instead show
existence of
all
pre-universal multimorphisms (not just nullary
and binary ones), and then show these are closed under composition;
this suffices for representability
by
[
Her00
, Proposition 8.5]
.

We begin with the
n
-ary analogue of
5.2.1
.

.

Let

Lemma 5.3.3
.

The commuting tensor product functor

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{i}\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})[(A_{i},a_{i}),(B_{i},b_{i})]}

Colimits commute with colimits and all the functors involved in

preserve reflexive coequalisers.

∎

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F\big(Fp_{1}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes Fp_{m}\big)}

Remark 5.3.7
.

We proceeded in a different way from
[
DH14
]
, who
first define the commuting tensor product of free bimodules
and then extend it to all bimodules via a colimit diagram (see
[
DH14
, Equation (1.4)]
). Here, we first isolated the universal property
that the commuting tensor of bimodules should satisfy, by introducing the notion of a
commuting multimorphism of bimodules. The two constructions agree, as
the colimit is equivalent to the coequalizer in
Eq.

46
.

In a similar spirit to
3.3.11
and
4.3.6
, the desired symmetric monoidal structure on the horizontal category of
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
is now
immediate.

Proposition 5.3.8
.

The horizontal category
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})_{1}
of
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})

admits the structure of a symmetric monoidal category, with tensor product the commuting tensor product of bimodules.

Proof.

It is the underlying monoidal category of the symmetric multicategory of bimodules and commuting bimodule morphisms of
5.3.6
.
∎

5.4.
The symmetric normal oplax monoidal structure on
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})

respectively, as well as the rest of the data in
2.5.1

commuting tensor product. We begin by constructing these for free bimodules.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2},a_{1}\otimes a_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(C_{1}\boxtimes C_{2},c_{1}\otimes c_{2})}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2},b_{1}\otimes b_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(C_{1}\boxtimes C_{2},c_{1}\otimes c_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F(y_{1})\bullet F(x_{1}))\otimes(F(y_{2})\bullet F(x_{2}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\xi^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(x_{1})\otimes F(x_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(y_{1})\otimes F(y_{2})}

Proof.

For the bimodule at the top of the diagram, we have an isomorphism

\displaystyle(F_{b_{1},c_{1}}(y_{1})\bullet F_{a_{1},b_{1}}(x_{1}))\otimes(F_{b_{2},c_{2}}(y_{2})\bullet F_{a_{2},b_{2}}(x_{2}))

\displaystyle\cong F_{a_{1},c_{1}}(y_{1}\circ b_{1}\circ x_{1})\otimes F_{a_{2},c_{2}}(y_{2}\circ b_{2}\circ x_{2})

\displaystyle\cong F_{a_{1}\otimes a_{2},c_{1}\otimes c_{2}}((y_{1}\circ b_{1}\circ x_{1})\boxtimes(y_{2}\circ b_{2}\circ x_{2}))

given by
Eq.

12
and
Eq.

48
, respectively.
For the composite bimodules at the bottom of the diagram, we have an isomorphism

\displaystyle\big(F_{b_{1},c_{1}}(y_{1})\otimes F_{b_{2},c_{2}}(y_{2})\big)\bullet\big(F_{a_{1},b_{1}}(x_{1})\otimes F_{a_{2},b_{2}}(x_{2})\big)

\displaystyle\cong\big(F_{b_{1}\otimes b_{2},c_{1}\otimes c_{2}}(y_{1}\boxtimes y_{2})\big)\bullet\big(F_{a_{1}\otimes a_{2},b_{1}\otimes b_{2}}(x_{1}\boxtimes x_{2})\big)

\displaystyle\cong F_{a_{1}\otimes a_{2},c_{1}\otimes c_{2}}\big((y_{1}\boxtimes y_{2})\circ(b_{1}\otimes b_{2})\circ(x_{1}\boxtimes x_{2})\big)

where we used
Eq.

48
and
Eq.

12
, respectively.
Therefore, the required globular bimodule 2-morphism
\xi^{\prime}
is given by composing these bimodule isomorphisms with the 2-morphism obtained by applying the free

(c_{1}\otimes c_{2},a_{1}\otimes a_{2})
-bimodule functor
F_{a_{1}\otimes a_{2},c_{1}\otimes c_{2}}
to the composite 2-morphism

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}\boxtimes C_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}\boxtimes C_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}\boxtimes C_{2}\mathrlap{,}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(y_{1}\circ b_{1}\circ x_{1})\boxtimes(y_{2}\circ b_{2}\circ x_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\xi}

where
\xi
is the interchange for
\mathbb{C}
and

is the comparison 2-cell in
Eq.

.

. Then, there is no reason for which
the interchange map for these bimodules

\tilde{\xi}\colon(a_{1}\bullet a_{1})\otimes(q_{2}\bullet p_{2})\to(a_{1}\otimes q_{2})\bullet(a_{1}\otimes p_{2})

constructed as in (

) should be an isomorphism.
This is essentially because the map
(\ast\ast)
of (
50
), which has the form

(Fa_{1}\bullet Fa_{1})\otimes(Fq_{2}\bullet Fp_{2})\xrightarrow{\xi^{\prime}}(Fa_{1}\otimes Fq_{2})\bullet(Fa_{1}\otimes Fp_{2})

does not seem to be an isomorphism either. Indeed, the latter is obtained by composing isomorphisms with the result
of applying the free bimodule functor to the 2-morphism

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}\boxtimes C_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}\boxtimes C_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\boxtimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\boxtimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}\boxtimes C_{2}\mathrlap{,}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(a_{1}\circ a_{1}\circ a_{1})\boxtimes(a_{2}\circ b_{2}\circ p_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\xi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{1}\boxtimes p_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{1}\boxtimes b_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\pi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{1}\boxtimes q_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{1}\boxtimes p_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{1}\otimes b_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{1}\boxtimes q_{2}}

which is not invertible in general, as it involves the interchange of
\mathbb{C}
on non-identity maps.
Attempting to present
(a_{1}\bullet a_{1})\otimes(q_{2}\bullet p_{2})
with a different
coequaliser than the one on the left-hand side of (
50
),
exploiting that some of the bimodules involved are identity bimodules, runs into the same issue.

Since the oplax monoidal structure of
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
does not seem to be normal, we do not extract a symmetric monoidal structure on the horizontal bicategory of
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C})
(see
[
GGV24
, Section 4]
for details). Far from being a problem, this subtle aspect provides extra motivation for our double categorical approach.

6.
Applications

In this last section, we present two applications of our theory.
The first one recovers the known fact that the tensor product of (enriched) categories extends to a symmetric monoidal structure on the double category of (enriched) profunctors. The second one establishes
a new result, which is obtained by replacing (enriched) categories by (enriched) symmetric
multicategories, and profunctors by bimodules between multicategories – which we here refer to as symmetric multiprofunctors (see
6.2.7
for details). More precisely, we show that the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of (enriched) symmetric multicategories (see e.g.
[
EM09
]
) extends to a symmetric oplax monoidal structure on the double category of symmetric multiprofunctors.

6.1.
Categories and profunctors

Let
\mathcal{V}
be a symmetric monoidal closed and locally presentable category. We write
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
for the double category of
\mathcal{V}
-matrices,
as considered in our running example (starting in
2.1.2
).
Although we have presented many aspects of this example in the course
of the paper, we give a self-contained treatment here, both for the
reader’s convenience, and also in order to highlight the structural
similarities with our second application to follow. In particular, in

6.1.1
and
6.1.2
below, we re-verify the
fact that
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
satisfies all the assumptions required to apply our general results, building on
[
ASV24
,
GGV24
]
. We begin by establishing the symmetric monoidal closed structure. Note that this is a genuine monoidal structure, rather than an oplax one.

Lemma 6.1.1
.

The double category
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
of
\mathcal{V}
-matrices admits a symmetric monoidal closed
structure, given on objects by the cartesian product of sets.

Proof.

This is
[
ASV24
, Examples 3.2.2 and 3.2.12]
, but we recall some
definitions in preparation for our second application in
Section

6.2
.
The vertical category of
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
is
\mathsf{Set}
, which is cartesian closed. We write
\langle B,C\rangle
for the set of functions between
B
and
C
and
\lambda(f)\colon A\to\langle B,C\rangle
for the adjoint transpose of a function
f\colon A\times B\to C
.

This closed structure can be extended to the horizontal category of
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
. For
x\colon A\hbox to38pt{\vbox to5.6pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 18.99997pt\lower-0.5pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{}{}{}{}{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}}{{}}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{}{{
{}{}}}{
{}{}}
{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-22.0pt}{0.0pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}}}{{}}{{}}}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
{
{}{}{}}{}{
{}{}{}}

are in
\mathcal{V}
.

To conclude the proof that the symmetric monoidal structure of the horizontal category of
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
is closed, one needs to show that there is a bijection between 2-morphisms on the left and on the right:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\times B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}\times B^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}\mathrlap{,}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x\otimes y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces z}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle B,C\rangle}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle B^{\prime},C^{\prime}\rangle\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda(f)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ \scriptstyle\Downarrow\psi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda(f^{\prime})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle y,z\rangle}

To see this, note that a 2-morphism
\phi
as above has components of the form

\phi_{(a^{\prime},b^{\prime}),(a,b)}\colon x[a^{\prime};a]\otimes y[b^{\prime};b]\to z[f^{\prime}(a^{\prime},b^{\prime});f(a,b)]\mathrlap{,}

while a 2-morphism like
\psi
has components of the form

\psi_{a,a^{\prime}}\colon x(a^{\prime},a)\to\prod_{b\in B,b^{\prime}\in B^{\prime}}\big[y[b^{\prime};b],z[f^{\prime}(a^{\prime},b^{\prime});f(a,b)]\big]\mathrlap{,}

see
[
Vas19
, Proposition 4.3]
for more details.
∎

The next lemma deals with structure of the double category
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
required to apply
the general theory of the previous sections, as detailed already in
Table

2
.

Lemma 6.1.2
.

The double category
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}

satisfies
I
,
II
,
III
,
IV
,
V
,
VI
,
VII
and
VIII
.

Proof.

We need to check that:

(1)

\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
is fibrant,

(2)

each
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}})
has coproducts,

(3)

(\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}})_{0}
has equalisers,

(4)

\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
has 1-tabulators,

(5)

each forgetful functor
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}})\to\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}})
has a left adjoint,

(6)

each
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}})
has local coequalisers,

(7)

\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
has local equalisers,

(8)

\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
has stable local reflexive coequalisers.

Part (I) is well-known.
For part (III), note that
(\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}})_{0}=\mathsf{Set}
. The existence of 1-tabulators (
2.4.5
) as required for part (IV) is known, and was discussed in
2.4.6
.

Next, recall that, for sets
A
and
B
, the category
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}[A,B]
defined in (
3
) is locally
presentable. In particular,
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
has local equalisers, giving us (VII).
From the proof of
[
ASV24
, Proposition 3.4.8]
,
local small colimits in
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
are stable. In particular, (VIII) holds.
Furthermore, (V) holds by known results on free monoids
[
Kel80
,
Lac10
]
, since e.g. each category
\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}})=\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}(A\times A,\mathcal{V})
has countable coproducts preserved by horizontal composition
in each variable.
It follows from this and fibrancy that
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
has free monads (
2.2.4
)
(see also comments below
2.2.4
). But now, since

\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
has stable local reflexive coequalisers, free monads, and local small colimits,

\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}})
has local small colimits by part (iii) of
2.4.3

(see also comments below
2.4.2
and
2.4.3
).
In particular, we obtain (II) and (VI).
∎

Theorem 6.1.3
.

Let
\mathcal{V}
be a symmetric monoidal closed locally presentable category.
The double category
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
of
\mathcal{V}
-categories,
\mathcal{V}
-functors, and
\mathcal{V}
-profunctors admits a symmetric monoidal structure, given on objects by the tensor product of
\mathcal{V}
-categories.

Proof.

This is an application of
5.4.2
, in this case where the oplax monoidal double structure is actually (pseudo) monoidal. The hypotheses are verified
in
6.1.1
and
6.1.2
. A direct calculation shows that a monad multimorphism
is commuting if and only if it is a
\mathcal{V}
-functor in many variables. Hence, the commuting
tensor coincides with the tensor product of
\mathcal{V}
-categories.
∎

As noted in
2.5.3
, we may generalise the above from
the familiar situation of a symmetric monoidal base
\mathcal{V}
to that
of a normal duoidal base
\mathcal{V}
; on doing so, we reconstruct exactly
the “many-object” theory of commuting tensor products of

\mathcal{V}
-categories over such a base given in
[
GL16
]
.

Corollary 6.1.4
.

The bicategory of
\mathcal{V}
-categories,
\mathcal{V}
-profunctors, and
\mathcal{V}
-natural transformations
admits a symmetric monoidal structure, given on objects as the tensor product of
\mathcal{V}
-categories.

Proof.

This follows from
6.1.3
via
[
GGV24
]
.
∎

6.2.
Symmetric multicategories and symmetric multiprofunctors

We now consider a locally presentable category
\mathcal{V}
, which we view as symmetric monoidal with respect to its finite products. The restriction
to cartesian monoidal structure was already imposed in
[
GGV24

in order to construct the

of categorical symmetric sequences, namely the oplax monoidal structure of our base double category

First of all, we set up some preliminary notation. Let

\mathcal{V}

\mathcal{V}
-category on

.

where, for

\vec{a}^{\prime}\boxtimes\vec{b}^{\prime}=\big((a^{\prime}_{1},b^{\prime}_{1}),(a^{\prime}_{2},b^{\prime}_{1}),\ldots,(a^{\prime}_{m},b_{1}),\ldots,(a^{\prime}_{1},b^{\prime}_{n}),\ldots,(a^{\prime}_{m},b^{\prime}_{n})\big)\mathrlap{.}

The next two lemmas check that
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
satifies the assumptions needed to apply our general theory, expanding on
[
GGV24
, Theorem 10.9]
. The first one is analogous to the previous

6.1.1
.
Note that the closed structure generalises the divided power closed structure of
[

]

.

Lemma 6.2.1
.

The double category
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
of categorical symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-sequences admits a symmetric normal oplax monoidal closed structure,
given on horizontal maps by the arithmetic product of categorical symmetric sequences.

Proof.

The normal oplax monoidal structure of
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
is
[
GGV24
, Theorem 10.9]
.
The symmetry of the tensor product is straightforward.

For the closure of the monoidal structure, first note that the vertical fragment of
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
is
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
and that the arithmetic tensor product therein coincides with the tensor product of
\mathcal{V}
-categories, which is well-known to be part of a cartesian closed monoidal structure (as
\mathcal{V}
is cartesian monoidal) whose internal hom is given by functor
\mathcal{V}
-categories, written
\langle B,C\rangle
here. For
f\colon A\boxtimes B\to C
, we write
\lambda(f)\colon A\to\langle B,C\rangle
for its adjoint transpose.

Next, we extend this to the horizontal category of
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
. For
y\colon B\rightsquigarrow B^{\prime}
and
z\colon C\rightsquigarrow C^{\prime}
,
we define
\langle y,z\rangle\colon\langle B,C\rangle\rightsquigarrow\langle B^{\prime},C^{\prime}\rangle
by letting, for

(g^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,g^{\prime}_{m})\in S\langle B^{\prime},C^{\prime}\rangle
and
g\in\langle B,C\rangle
,

(55)

\langle y,z\rangle[g^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,g^{\prime}_{m};g]\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\\
\prod_{n\in\mathsf{N}}\int_{(b^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,b^{\prime}_{n})\in S_{n}B^{\prime}}\int_{b\in B}\Big[y[b^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,b^{\prime}_{n};b],\ z\big[g^{\prime}_{1}(b^{\prime}_{1}),\ldots,g^{\prime}_{1}(b^{\prime}_{n}),\ldots,g^{\prime}_{m}(b^{\prime}_{1}),\ldots,g^{\prime}_{m}(b^{\prime}_{n});g(b)\big]\Big]

using the internal hom of
\mathcal{V}
. Observe that
y[b^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,b^{\prime}_{n};b]
and
z\big[g^{\prime}_{1}(b^{\prime}_{1}),\ldots,g^{\prime}_{1}(b^{\prime}_{n}),\ldots,g^{\prime}_{m}(b^{\prime}_{1}),\ldots,g^{\prime}_{m}(b^{\prime}_{n});g(b)\big]
are objects in
\mathcal{V}
.

To conclude the proof that horizontal category of
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
is closed, one needs to show that,
with the definitions above, there is a bijection between 2-cells on the left and on the right, as below:

(56)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxtimes B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}\boxtimes B^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}\mathrlap{,}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x\boxtimes y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces z}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle B,C\rangle}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle B^{\prime},C^{\prime}\rangle\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda(f)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\psi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda(f^{\prime})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle y,z\rangle}

By the definition of 2-morphisms in
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}

Eq.

52
, a 2-morphism
\phi
as on the left is a
\mathcal{V}
-natural transformation with components of the form

\phi_{\vec{u}^{\prime},(a,b)}\colon(x\boxtimes y)[\vec{u};(a,b)]\to z[(Sf^{\prime})(\vec{u}^{\prime});f(a,b)]\mathrlap{,}

for
\vec{u}^{\prime}\in S(A^{\prime}\boxtimes B^{\prime})
and
(a,b)\in A\boxtimes B
. The domain of these maps is defined explicitly in (
54
).
Instead, a 2-morphism
\psi
as on the right above is a
\mathcal{V}
-natural transformation with components of the form

(57)

\psi_{\vec{a}^{\prime},a}\colon x[\vec{a}^{\prime};a]\to\langle y,z\rangle[S(\lambda f^{\prime})(\vec{a}^{\prime});\lambda f(a)]

for
\vec{a}^{\prime}\in SA^{\prime}
and
a\in A
. Note that
\lambda f(a)\in\langle B,C\rangle
and
S(\lambda f^{\prime})(\vec{a}^{\prime})\in S\langle B^{\prime},C^{\prime}\rangle
. The former is simply the
\mathcal{V}
-functor
f(a,-)
. The latter, for
\vec{a}^{\prime}=(a_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,a_{m}^{\prime})
, is the
m
-tuple of
\mathcal{V}
-functors
(f^{\prime}(a^{\prime}_{1},-),\ldots,f^{\prime}(a^{\prime}_{m},-))
. Hence, the codomain of the map in (
57
) can be simplified to

\langle y,z\rangle\big[f^{\prime}(a^{\prime}_{1},-),\ldots,f^{\prime}(a_{m},-);f(a,-)]\mathrlap{.}

This, by the definition in (
55
), is

\prod_{n\in\mathsf{N}}\int_{\vec{b}^{\prime}\in S_{n}B^{\prime}}\int_{b\in B}\Big[y[\vec{b}^{\prime};b],\ z\big[(Sf^{\prime})(\vec{a}^{\prime}\boxtimes\vec{b}^{\prime});f(a,b)\big]\Big]\mathrlap{.}

The required bijection now follows by a direct calculation with ends and coends which we omit.

In order for the monoidal closed structure on the vertical and horizontal fragment of the double category
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
to form an oplax monoidal
closed
double structure, as in

2.5.5
one should also verify that the source and target functors commute
with the definitions of the closed structures, and that the evaluation square of the closed structure on
(\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}})_{1}
should have the evaluations of the closed structure on
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
as vertical maps, as in

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle B,C\rangle\boxtimes B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle B^{\prime}\boxtimes C^{\prime}\rangle\boxtimes B^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle y,z\rangle\boxtimes y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{ev}_{B,C}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\mathsf{ev}_{y,z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{ev}_{B^{\prime},C^{\prime}}^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces z}

These hold by the very definition of
\mathsf{ev}_{y,z}
as the transpose of the identity on
\langle y,z\rangle

across the bijection in (
56
).
We leave these routine calculations to the readers.
∎

Remark 6.2.2
.

Just as the arithmetic product of categorical symmetric sequences defined in (
54
) generalises the arithmetic product of single-sorted symmetric sequences defined in
[
DH14
]
, the monoidal closed structure defined above generalises
the
divided power
closed structure defined therein. Indeed, if we take
A=B=C=1
above, the formula for
\langle y,z\rangle
reduces to the end

\langle y,z\rangle(m)\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\int_{n\in S1}\big[y(n),z(m\times n)\big]\mathrlap{.}

In particular, note that the first argument of
z
in (
55
) is a sequence of length

m\times n
.

We move on to the rest of the assumptions on the double category of symmetric sequences (
Table

2
), that allow for our general theory from the previous sections to be applied.
The proof of
6.2.3
is similar to that of
6.1.2
, but
there is an important difference: in our current setting, we do not have stability of all local small colimits, but only of
sifted ones (and in particular reflexive coequalisers). This was one of the reasons for working
with
VIII
, rather than stronger versions thereof.

Lemma 6.2.3
.

The double category
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
satisfies

I
,
II
,
III
,
IV
,
V
,
VI
,
VII
and
VIII
.

Proof.

We need to check the following:

(1)

\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
is fibrant,

(2)

each
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}})
has coproducts,

(3)

(\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}})_{0}
has equalisers,

(4)

\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
has 1-tabulators,

(5)

each forgetful functor
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}})\to\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}})
has a left adjoint,

(6)

each
\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}})
has coequalisers,

(7)

\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
has local equalisers,

(8)

\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
has stable local reflexive coequalisers.

Part (I) can be proved along the lines of
[
GGV24
, Proposition 9.3]
or by direct calculation.
For part (III), observe that
(\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}})_{0}=\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
.
For part (IV), according to
2.4.5
given a categorical symmetric sequence
x\colon A\rightsquigarrow B
, its 1-tabulator
Tx
is given by
the
\mathcal{V}
-category whose set of objects is

\coprod_{a\in A,b\in B}\mathcal{V}(I,x[(b);a])\mathrlap{.}

The morphisms of its underlying category
(f,g)\colon(a^{\prime},b^{\prime},u^{\prime})\to(a,b,u)
are pairs consisting of
f\colon a^{\prime}\to a

and
g\colon b^{\prime}\to b
such that
u\cdot g=u^{\prime}\cdot f
. The hom-objects
Tx((a^{\prime},b^{\prime},u^{\prime}),(a,b,u))\in\mathcal{V}

are given by a corresponding equaliser. The functors
\pi_{\mathfrak{s}}\colon Tx\to A
and
\pi_{\mathfrak{s}}\colon Tx\to B
are the two evident projections. For the 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Tx}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Tx}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{Tx}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{\mathfrak{s}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\pi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{\mathfrak{t}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}

we need a
\mathcal{V}
-natural transformation
\pi\colon\mathrm{id}_{Tx}\to x\circ(S\pi_{\mathfrak{t}}\times\pi_{\mathfrak{s}})
.
By the definition of horizontal maps in
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
, the only non-trivial components of
such a transformation are of the form

\pi_{((a^{\prime},b^{\prime},u^{\prime})),(a,b,u)}\colon Tx\big((a^{\prime},b^{\prime},u^{\prime}),(a,b,u)\big)\to x[(b^{\prime});a]\mathrlap{,}

which are defined by sending
(f,g)\colon(a^{\prime},b^{\prime},u^{\prime})\to(a,b,u)
to
u\cdot g
(or, equivalently,
u^{\prime}\cdot f)
.

Next, recall that, for
\mathcal{V}
-categories
A
and
B
, the category
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}[A,B]
defined in (
53
) is locally
presentable. In particular,
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
has local equalisers, giving us (VII).
Also, by
[
GJ17
, Corollary 4.4.9]
, composition in the horizontal bicategory of
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}

preserves all colimits in the first variable and sifted colimits in the second variable.
This implies (VIII) by
2.4.1
, as reflexive coequalisers are sifted colimits, and (V) by known results on free monoids
[
Kel80
,
Lac10
]
applied to
\mathsf{End}_{A}(\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}})=\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}(SA^{\mathrm{op}}\otimes A,\mathcal{V})
.
It follows from (V) and fibrancy that
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
has free monads (
2.2.6
). But now, since

\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
has stable local reflexive coequalisers, free monads, local
coproducts, and local reflexive coequalisers, each

\mathsf{Mnd}_{A}(\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}})
has coproducts and reflexive coequalisers by part (iii) of
2.4.3
, thus giving us (II) and (VI).
∎

Remark 6.2.4
.

Let us note that the definition of the double category
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
and the
properties in
6.2.3
hold for a general symmetric monoidal category

\mathcal{V}
, while the assumption that the monoidal structure is cartesian is needed for

6.2.1
.

Monads in
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
are the
symmetric substitutes
of
[
DS03a
,
DS03b
]
,
which are similar to symmetric multicategories, the main differerence being that they have a category, rather than a mere set, of objects, whose maps can be thought of as a distinguished set of unary morphisms in a
symmetric multicategory. In preparation for our main application is to multicategories, we record the following:

Theorem 6.2.5
.

Let
\mathcal{V}
be locally presentable cartesian closed category, considered as a cartesian monoidal category.
The double category
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}})
of symmetric substitutes and their bimodules
admits an symmetric oplax monoidal closed structure.

Proof.

This follows from
5.4.2
, which we can apply thanks to

6.2.1
and
6.2.3
.
∎

We define the double category of symmetric sequences
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
as the full double subcategory of
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
spanned by sets, viewed as discrete
\mathcal{V}
-categories, so that there is an inclusion

(58)

\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}\mathrlap{.}

Monads in
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
are exactly symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multicategories (cf.
[
BD98
]
). Indeed, a monad
(A,a)
in
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
gives a symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multicategory with set of objects
A
and hom-objects
a[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n};x]\in\mathcal{V}
, for
x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},x\in A
. The composition is given by the multiplication of the monad and the identity maps are given by the unit of the monad. Conversely, given a symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multicategory
A
, we obtain a monad in
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
with
underlying set the set of objects of
A
and symmetric sequence
\mathrm{hom}_{A}\colon A\hbox to38pt{\vbox to5.6pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 18.99997pt\lower-0.5pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{}{}{}{}{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}}{{}}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{}{{

.
See
[
GJ17
, Example 4.1.4]
for more details. Furthermore, the free monad on a symmetric sequence is exactly the free symmetric multicategory on it. From now on, we will identify monads
in
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
with symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multicategories and simply write
A,B,C,\ldots
to denote them.

Lemma 6.2.6
.

\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
is fibrant and has stable local reflexive coequalisers.

Proof.

The required structure and properties were established for
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
in
6.2.3
and it is clear that they restrict to
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}
along the inclusion in (
58
).
∎

Thanks to
6.2.6
, we can consider the double category
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}})
. The inclusion in
Eq.

58
induces a commutative diagram of inclusions

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}})\mathrlap{.}}

We define

\mathbb{S}\mathsf{MultProf}_{\mathcal{V}}=\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}})

and refer to
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{MultProf}_{\mathcal{V}}
as the
double category of symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multiprofunctors
.
Indeed, as we explain below,
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{MultProf}_{\mathcal{V}}
is the analogue for symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multicategories of the double category
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
of
\mathcal{V}
-categories,
\mathcal{V}
-functors and
\mathcal{V}
-profunctors.

We describe explicitly
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{MultProf}_{\mathcal{V}}
. As mentioned, its objects are symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multicategories.
Similarly, the vertical maps of
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}})
are symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multifunctors. Thus, the vertical category of
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}})
is the category
\mathsf{SMultCat}_{\mathcal{V}}
of symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multicategories and symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multifunctors. The horizontal maps of
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{im}(\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}})
were called bimodules in
[
GJ17
]
, but we prefer to refer to them as
symmetric multiprofunctors
in order to emphasize the analogy with profunctors. We unfold the definition for the convenience of the readers.

Definition 6.2.7
.

Let
A
and
B
be symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multicategories. A
symmetric

\mathcal{V}
-multiprofunctor

p\colon A\rightsquigarrow B
consists of

(1)

for every
a\in A
and
(b_{1},\ldots,b_{n})\in SB
, an object

p[b_{1},\ldots,b_{n};a]\in\mathcal{V}\mathrlap{,}

subject to equivariance conditions, so as to give a symmetric sequence
p\colon A\rightsquigarrow B
;

(2)

for every
\vec{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n})\in SA
,
\vec{b}_{1},\ldots,\vec{b}_{n}\in SB
, and
a\in A
,
a map

\rho_{\vec{a},\vec{b}_{1},\ldots,\vec{b}_{n},a}\colon p[\vec{b}_{1};a_{1}]\otimes\cdots\otimes p[\vec{b}_{n};a_{n}]\otimes\mathrm{hom}_{A}[\vec{a};a]\to p[\vec{b}_{1}\oplus\ldots\oplus\vec{b}_{n};a]\mathrlap{,}

subject to equivariance conditions, so as to give a right action
\rho\colon p\circ\mathrm{hom}_{A}\Rightarrow p
;

(3)

for every
\vec{b}=(b_{1},\ldots,b_{n})\in SB
,
\vec{b}_{1},\ldots,\vec{b}_{n}\in SB
, and
a\in A
,
a map

\lambda_{\vec{b},\vec{b}_{1},\ldots,\vec{b}_{n},a}\colon\mathrm{hom}_{B}[\vec{b}_{1};b_{1}]\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathrm{hom}_{B}[\vec{b}_{n};b_{n}]\otimes p[\vec{b};a]\to p[\vec{b}_{1}\oplus\ldots\oplus\vec{b}_{n};a]\mathrlap{,}

subject to equivariance conditions, so as to give a left action
\lambda\colon\mathrm{hom}_{B}\circ p\Rightarrow p
;

satisfying the bimodule compatibility conditions in
2.3.1
.

Just as the values
f\in p[b;a]
of a profunctor
p\colon A\to B
between categories can be understood as heterogenous morphisms
f\colon b\to a
, the values
f\colon p[b_{1},\ldots,b_{n};a]
of a symmetric multiprofunctor

p\colon A\rightsquigarrow B
between symmetric multicategories can be understood as heterogenous multimorphisms

f\colon b_{1},\ldots b_{n}\to a
. From this point of view, the data in parts (ii) and (iii)
6.2.7

can be readily understood as describing how to compose such multimorphisms
with the multimorphisms of
A
and of
B
, respectively. The equivariance, associativity,
unitality and bimodule compatibility conditions are then rather natural laws to impose on such
composition operations. As typical in this subject, these operations can be vividly represented
in terms of grafting operations on trees. Observe that the notation
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{MultProf}_{\mathcal{V}}
follows our convention of naming bimodule double categories by the name of their horizontal maps.

We now obtain the main application of our general theory.

Theorem 6.2.8
.

Let
\mathcal{V}
be locally presentable cartesian closed category, considered as a cartesian monoidal category.
The double category
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{MultProf}_{\mathcal{V}}
of symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multicategories, symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multifunctors
and symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multiprofunctors
admits a symmetric oplax monoidal closed structure, given on objects by the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multicategories.

Proof.

This follows from
6.2.5
by observing that the
commuting tensor product of symmetric substitutes restricts to the Boardman–Vogt tensor
product of symmetric multicategories.
∎

Remark 6.2.9
.

Part of
6.2.8
is the statement that the vertical category of
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{MultProf}_{\mathcal{V}}

admits a symmetric monoidal structure, which is in fact closed by
4.3.6
.
This recovers the known fact that
\mathsf{SMultCat}_{\mathcal{V}}
admit a symmetric monoidal closed structure.
In fact, by
3.3.11
, this category admits also a non-commuting tensor product,
which was constructed in
[
EM09
]
and should be regarded as the counterpart for symmetric

\mathcal{V}
-multicategories of the funny tensor product of
\mathcal{V}
-categories.
Compare also the pushout in
Eq.

19
with
[
EM09
, Construction 4.10]
.

We write
\mathbb{O}\mathsf{pdBim}_{\mathcal{V}}
for the full double subcategory of
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{MultProf}_{\mathcal{V}}
spanned by symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-multicategories with one object, which are the same thing as
\mathcal{V}
-operads
[
Kel05
,
May72
]
. Following the terminology in the literature, we refer to
the horizontal maps of
\mathbb{O}\mathsf{pdBim}_{\mathcal{V}}
as bimodules. An explicit definition of this notion can be readily obtained
by instantiating
6.2.7
taking
A
and
B
therein to be operads, but we do not spell it out.
Our final theorem shows that the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of operads extends to a
symmetric normal oplax monoidal closed structure on
\mathbb{O}\mathsf{pdBim}_{\mathcal{V}}
.

Theorem 6.2.10
.

Let
\mathcal{V}
be locally presentable category, considered as a cartesian symmetric monoidal category.
The double category
\mathbb{O}\mathsf{pdBim}_{\mathcal{V}}
of symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-operads, symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-operad morphisms, and symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-operad
bimodules admits a symmetric oplax monoidal closed structure, given by the Boardman–Vogt tensor product.

Proof.

This follows by
6.2.8
observing that the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of
symmetric multicategories restricts to operads.
∎

While the definition of the Boardman–Vogt tensor product symmetric multicategories goes back to
[
BV73
]
and its definition on operad bimodules to
[
DH14
]
,
the interaction between the Boardman–Vogt tensor product and the composition operation of bimodules isolated in
6.2.8
and
6.2.10

appears to be new. For operads, this amounts to the fact that,
given operad bimodules
p_{1}\colon A_{1}\rightsquigarrow B_{1}
and
p_{2}\colon A_{2}\rightsquigarrow B_{2}
,

q_{1}\colon B_{1}\rightsquigarrow C_{1}
and
q_{2}\colon B_{2}\rightsquigarrow C_{2}
, we have an operad morphism

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\otimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}\otimes C_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}\otimes A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}\otimes B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{1}\otimes C_{2}\mathrlap{,}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(q_{1}\bullet p_{1})\otimes(q_{2}\bullet p_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\xi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}\otimes p_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{1}\otimes q_{2}}

satisfying appropriate coherence conditions. As discussed in
5.4.3
, we do not expect the oplax monoidal structures of
6.2.8
and
6.2.10

to be normal. Hence, the Boardman–Vogt tensor product does not seem to yield a
symmetric monoidal oplax structure on the horizontal bicategories of
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{MultProf}_{\mathcal{V}}
and
\mathbb{O}\mathsf{pdBim}_{\mathcal{V}}
. Happily, the double categories
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{MultProf}_{\mathcal{V}}
and
\mathbb{O}\mathsf{pdBim}_{\mathcal{V}}

have instead a genuine symmetric oplax monoidal structure.
